It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿ولَقَدْ جاءَكَ مِن نَبَأِ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ [al-An'am: 34] ("And certainly there has come to you some of the news of the messengers") in Surah al-An'am, and His saying: ﴿قُلْ هو نَبَأٌ عَظِيمٌ أنْتُمْ عَنْهُ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾ [Sad: 67-68] ("Say: It is a great news, from which you turn away").

The word ﴿العَظِيمُ﴾ (al-'aẓīm) literally means "large in body," and it is used figuratively for an important matter, because the importance of a meaning is imagined through the largeness of a body, in that it falls upon the mind of the one who recalls it, just as the sight of a large body falls upon the eye. This figurative usage became so widespread that it equaled the literal meaning.

Describing the naba' as ﴿العَظِيمُ﴾ here is an increase in drawing attention to it, because its being sent from the unseen world increased it in greatness of qualities and terrors. So the naba' is described as great in view of what was described in it of the states of the Resurrection in what was revealed of the verses of the Qur'an before this. A parallel to this is the Most High's saying: ﴿قُلْ هو نَبَأٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [Sad: 67] ﴿أنْتُمْ عَنْهُ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾ [Sad: 68] in Surah Sad.

The definite article in ﴿النَّبَأِ﴾ is the definite article of the genus (ta'rīf al-jins), so it includes every great news that the Messenger (ﷺ) informed them of. The first of that is his informing them that the Qur'an is the speech of God, and what the Qur'an included of the refutation of polytheism, and of the affirmation of the resurrection of people on the Day of Resurrection. What is related from some of the early generation about specifying a particular news is taken as an illustration: from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the Qur'an; and from Mujahid and Qatadah: it is the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection.

The argument drawn from His saying: ﴿ألَمْ نَجْعَلِ الأرْضَ مِهادًا﴾ [al-Naba': 6] ("Have We not made the earth a resting place?") up to His saying: ﴿وجَنّاتٍ ألْفافًا﴾ [al-Naba': 16] ("and gardens of dense growth") clearly indicates that what is meant by the "great news" is the announcement that God is one and has no partner.

The nominal sentence was used in the relative clause, rather than saying "the one about which they disagree" or something similar, so that the nominal sentence indicates that the disagreement about this news is firmly established among them and constant in them, since the nominal sentence indicates permanence and stability.

[p. 7]

The opening of the speech with a question about a group's mutual questioning concerning a great news item is an opening that arouses interest and then awe for what will be mentioned after it. It is therefore one of the striking openings, because of its rare and unfamiliar style, and because it arouses interest through the method of summary followed by detail, which best fixes the coming report in the listener's mind.

Since this opening signals a matter of great importance, it signals that a decisive word will be given about it. Since this includes an indication of the most important thing about which they were disputing that day, opening the speech with it is an instance of excellence in introduction (barā'at al-istihlāl).

The expression ﴿عَمَّ﴾ (ʿammā) is composed of two words: the preposition ﴿عَنْ﴾ ('an), and ﴿ما﴾ (mā), which is an interrogative noun meaning "what?" The phrase ﴿عَمَّ﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ (yatasā'alūna), so this is a compound. Its original order was ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ عَنْ ما﴾; the interrogative noun was placed first because it can only occur at the beginning of the interrogative sentence. Since the interrogative noun was attached to the preposition through which the verb reaches the interrogative noun, and since the preposition cannot be separated from its object, the two were placed together, becoming ﴿عَمّا يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾.

Eloquent usage has established that when the interrogative ﴿ما﴾ is preceded by a preposition, the alif that ends it is dropped, to distinguish it from the relative ﴿ما﴾ (mā al-mawṣūlah).

Their pronunciation followed this usage. When they wrote the codices (maṣāḥif), they followed this distinction in writing, so they wrote the interrogative ﴿ما﴾ without an alif wherever it occurred, as in the Most High's saying: ﴿فِيمَ أنْتَ مِن ذِكْراها﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 43] (“About what are you concerned in mentioning it?”), ﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (“With what will you give me good news?”), ﴿لِمَ أذِنْتَ لَهم﴾ (“Why did you permit them?”), ﴿عَمَّ يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾, ﴿مِمَّ خُلِقَ﴾ (“From what was he created?”). For this reason, no one recited them with the alif affirmed except in the anomalous (shādhdh) readings.

Since the word ﴿ما﴾ remained on one letter after its alif was dropped, they adopted in the orthography of the Qur'an the practice of writing its remaining mīm joined to the letter ﴿عَنْ﴾. This is because, once the alif of ﴿ما﴾ was dropped, it remained on one letter and so resembled the letters of spelling (ḥurūf al-tahajjī). Since the preposition before ﴿ما﴾ ends with a nūn, and the nūn met the mīm of ﴿ما﴾, and the Arabs pronounce a sakin nūn followed by a mīm as a mīm, assimilating it into it, when the nūn was dropped in pronunciation, their orthography followed pronunciation by writing the word without the nūn. A parallel to this is the Most High's saying: ﴿مِمَّ خُلِقَ﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 5]. This is a good convention.

The word ﴿التَّساؤُلُ﴾ (al-tasā'ul) is of the form tafā'ul (reciprocal form). The essential meaning of the tafā'ul form is that the meaning of its root is issued from the agent to the object and similarly from the object to the agent. It also frequently occurs to indicate the repetition of the occurrence of what it is derived from, as in their saying: ﴿ساءَلَ﴾, meaning ﴿سَألَ﴾ ("to ask"). Al-Nabighah said:

"I ask about Su'da, though seven complete (periods) have passed after us over the open spaces of the house."

And Ruwaysh ibn Kathir al-Ta'i said:

"O rider who urges his mount onward, ask the Banu Asad what this sound is."

[p. 8]

It also comes to indicate the strength of the verb's issuing from the agent, as in their saying: ﴿عافاكَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("May God grant you well-being"). This is either a kinayah (metonymy) or a majāz (figurative usage). Its interpretation in the verse permits all three possibilities. This is through intending the metonymic meaning together with the explicit meaning, or through using the expression in both its literal and figurative senses. Both considerations are valid in eloquent speech, so there is no basis for prohibiting them.

Thus it may be used in its literal sense, so that some of them ask others with the questioning of one seeking knowledge, since at that time they were still in doubt about the truth of what they had been informed of; then their affair settled upon denial.

It may also be used in a figurative formal sense (al-majāz al-ṣūrī): they pretend to ask while being certain that what they are asking about does not occur, following the usage of the verb ﴿يَحْذَرُ﴾ (yaḥdharu) in the Most High's saying: ﴿يَحْذَرُ المُنافِقُونَ أنْ تُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُورَةٌ﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64] ("The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be revealed about them"). In that case, by the questioning they intend mockery.

The exegetes took two positions on both of these methods, each group preferring what it adopted. The correct approach is to interpret the verse according to both, since the polytheists varied in their denial. From Ibn 'Abbas: when the Qur'an was revealed, the Quraysh were speaking among themselves; some of them were believers and some were deniers.

Similar to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas is what is reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said that it is a question of mockery or astonishment, while they are in fact certain of denial.

As for real questioning (al-tasā'ul al-ḥaqīqī), it is that one of them asks another about some aspect of this news, and the one asked asks his questioner about another aspect of the news, since each one has a thought different from the other's. So one asks as one seeking confirmation, or as a question to uncover his belief, or about what the one who reports this news is described as. This is like what some of them said to others: ﴿أفْتَرى عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا أمْ بِهِ جِنَّةٌ﴾ [Saba': 8] ("Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?"), and another said: ﴿أإذا كُنّا تُرابًا وآباؤُنا أإنّا لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ [al-Naml: 67] ("When we and our fathers have become dust, shall we indeed be brought forth?") up to His saying: ﴿إنْ هَذا إلّا أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ [al-Naml: 68] ("This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples").

As for the formal questioning (al-tasā'ul al-ṣūrī), it is that some of them ask others about this news with a question of derision and mockery. One of them says: "Has the report of the Resurrection reached you?" and the other says to him: "Have you heard what he said?" So the application of the word "questioning" is literal, since it is established for such a inquiry, but their intention from it is not literal; rather it is derisive.

The interrogation with ﴿ما﴾ in His saying ﴿عَمَّ يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ is not a real interrogation. Rather it is used to arouse interest in receiving the report, like the Most High's saying: ﴿هَلْ أُنَبِّئُكم عَلى مَن تَنَزَّلُ الشَّياطِينُ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 221] ("Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?").

The one addressed by the interrogation is of the kind of address to an unspecified person.

The pronoun in ﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ may be the pronoun of a group of absent persons, meaning the polytheists, though no mention of them has preceded in this speech. However, their mention is repeated in the Qur'an, so they became known by intention from some of its pronouns and vague allusions, like the pronoun in the Most High's saying: ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ بِالحِجابِ﴾ [Sad: 32] ("until it was hidden behind the veil"), meaning the sun; and ﴿كَلّا إذا بَلَغَتِ التَّراقِيَ﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ("No! When it reaches the collar-bones"), meaning the soul. If you make the speech a case of iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), then the pronoun is that of a group of addressees.

Since the interrogation is used for other than seeking understanding, it is appropriate that it be followed by its answer with His saying: ﴿عَنِ النَّبَإ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("about the great news"). So its answer is used as an explanation of what was intended by the interrogation of generality, for the purpose of magnification. Thus the aspect of magnification is clarified. A parallel to this is the Most High's saying: ﴿هَلْ أُنَبِّئُكم عَلى مَن تَنَزَّلُ الشَّياطِينُ تَنَزَّلُ عَلى كُلِّ أفّاكٍ أثِيمٍ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 221-222] ("Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every lying sinner"). It is as if it were said: "They ask about the great news." From it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"To whom does the abode belong, emptied in Ma'an, between the heights of al-Yarmuk and al-Sammān?
That is the dwelling of the family of Jafnah in the ages, and it is the truth that the changing times turn."

The word ﴿النَّبَأ﴾ (al-naba') means "news." It was said that it means "news" absolutely, so it would be synonymous with the word "khabar." This is the usage adopted by the lexicons al-Qamus, al-Sihah and al-Lisan.

Al-Raghib said: "Naba' is a news report of great benefit, through which knowledge or a strong presumption is obtained. The word naba' is not applied to a report until it includes these three things and is true." End of quote. This is a good distinction. I do not think the eloquent writers used it except in the manner al-Raghib described. So a report about ordinary matters is not called naba'. This is what the sources of the usage of the word naba' in the speech of the eloquent indicate. I think that those who equated naba' with khabar considered that in some speech of people there occurs a laxity in using naba' in the sense of any khabar, through some kind of interpretation or metonymic majāz mursal by generalization and restriction. This became so common in speech that it became difficult to define the positions of the two words. However, the most eloquent speech does not fittingly come except according to the most precise positions of usage.

Kallā (a particle of rebuke and nullification) is a particle of repudiation and nullification of something that usually precedes it in speech. It requires the rejection of what is attributed to the one addressed and the nullification of what was attributed to him. Here it is a rebuke directed at those who ask about the great news (al-naba' al-'azim) about which they disagree, in accordance with the meanings that the questioning may bear, as mentioned earlier, and a nullification of what the phrase "yatasa'aluna" (they ask) contains of a questioning known to the listeners.

Thus the position of the sentence is that of an answer to a question, and for this reason it is disjoined (fusila) and not conjoined with a conjunction (lam tu'taf), because that is the manner of question and answer.

Although the speech is a report about them, they are the intended addressees of it, so the rebuke is directed at them in this respect.

The meaning: the nullification of the disagreement concerning that news and the denial of questioning about it, the questioning by which they intended mockery and the denial of its occurrence. That affirms the occurrence of what the news brought and that it is true, because the nullification of the denial of its occurrence leads to the affirmation of its occurrence.

The usual use of "kallā" is that it is followed by speech that clarifies what it has summarized of rebuke and nullification. For this reason it is followed here by His words: "sa-ya'lamun" (they will know). This is an increase in the nullification of their speech, by affirming that they will certainly come to be certain of its occurrence and will be punished for denying it. These are two kinds of knowledge that will be obtained by them after death: knowledge of the truth of the occurrence of resurrection (al-ba'th), and knowledge of the punishment for it.

For this reason the object of "sa-ya'lamun" is omitted, so that it covers both known matters. For at death they see what they will come to, as has come in the authentic hadith: "Indeed the disbeliever sees his seat, and it is said to him: 'This is your seat until you are resurrected'" (ﷺ). And in the hadith: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire." This is among the visions of the soul of the one buried, and it is among the spiritual unveilings (al-mukashafat al-ruhiyya). By it was interpreted His saying the Exalted: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6] ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 7].

Thus this nullification and what follows it contain an announcement that the Day of Resurrection is certain to occur, and they contain a threat. Its emphasis has been effected by the particle of the future (sa-), whose function is to bring the future near.

Among the beauties of this style in threatening is that it gives the impression that they will know the answer to their question, which they intended as evasion and mockery, and they presented it in the form of a request for an answer. So this answer is in the manner of the saying of people: "The answer is what you see, not what you hear."

Escalation in the threat and warning. Since "thumma" (then) conjoins the sentence, it indicates rank-based sequencing (al-tartib al-rutbi): the meaning of the sentence that follows is higher in rank with respect to the purpose than the content of the sentence before it. Since the sentence after "thumma" is like the sentence before "thumma," it is necessarily the case that the content of the sentence after "thumma" is higher in degree than the content of its counterpart. The meaning of the elevation of rank is that the content after "thumma" is stronger than the content of the sentence before "thumma," and this content is the warning. Since the verification of the occurrence of what is threatened has been conveyed by the verbal emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi), because the sentence after "thumma" emphasizes the sentence before it, the meaning of the elevation of rank in the second sentence is necessarily understood to be that what is threatened in the second instance is greater than what they reckon.

The pronoun in "sa-ya'lamun" (they will know) in both places follows the same pattern as the pronoun in "yatasa'alun" (they question each other) and the pronoun in "fihi mukhtalifun" (about which they differ), as mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 6:

﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾

Since the greatest news the Qur'an brought them was the nullification of the divinity of their idols and the affirmation of the recreation of their bodies, and these were the two matters that provoked their denial that it came from God, their conspiracy against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and their spreading of his denial, this resumptive statement came as an explanation of the general expression in His words: ﴿about the momentous news﴾ [al-Naba': 2] ﴿over which they are in disagreement﴾ [al-Naba': 3].

Its completion will come after it in His words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba': 17].

In these verses God gathered for them the evidence for His oneness through His exclusive act of creation, and for the possibility of the bodies being restored for resurrection after decay, since restoring them does not reach the level of bringing into being the great created things.

Because the sentence stands in the position of evidence, it was not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it.

The address is directed to those who deny the resurrection, and they are the ones addressed by the interrogative. It is therefore a case of iltifat (shift of address), because directing the speech carries the force of the pronoun of address, as shown by the conjunction of ﴿and We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba': 8] to it.

The interrogative in ﴿Have We not made﴾ is confirmative (taqriri), and it is a confirmation through a negative, as is most common in confirmative interrogative forms, where a negation follows, most often with the particle (lam). That negation serves as a kind of excuse for the one being confirmed, if he intends to deny. What is intended is the confirmation of the occurrence of making the earth a resting-place, not its negation by the negative particle, merely to emphasize the meaning of confirmation.

So the meaning is: Did We not make the earth a resting-place? For this reason it will be followed by the conjunction ﴿and We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba': 8]. This was already discussed at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33] in Surat al-Baqarah. They cannot do other than acknowledge it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾ [Luqman: 25]. The essential point of the argument from the first creation of great created things is that it indicates the possibility of the second creation of created things that are lower than the first, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], that is, the second, ﴿but most people do not know﴾ [Ghafir: 57].

The "making" of the earth means creating it in that state, because its being a resting-place is a condition present in it from the beginning of its creation and from the times of that condition's occurrence for it, before the creation of man, which none knows but God.

The meaning is: He created it in a state in which it is like a resting-place. The speech is therefore an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh).

The expression "made" (naj'al) is used rather than "created" (nakhluq), because being a resting-place is a state among its conditions, either at its creation or after it, unlike the act of creating, which usually relates to the essence or to the attribute constituting the essence, as in ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

Al-mihad, with a kasra on the mim, is the spread-out, prepared bed. The pattern fi'al in it indicates that its origin is a verbal noun that was named by it for emphasis. In the Qamus it is said that al-mihad may refer to the cradle that is made for a child. In either case it is a simile of the earth to it, since He made its surface easy for sitting upon, lying down, and especially walking. That is evidence of the perfection of creation and of facilitation for people. It is an argument that carries a expression of favour, and in that favour there is an indication of the wisdom of God, exalted is He, since He made the earth suitable for the creatures upon it. The One who made this creation is not incapable of creating bodies a second time after their decay.

The purpose of the expression of favour here is to remind them of God's grace, so that perhaps they will desist from obstinacy and turn to consider what the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them to, as a conveyance from God, exalted is He.

The reason for beginning the argument for the possibility of resurrection with the creation of the earth is that resurrection is the bringing forth of the people of the gathering from the earth, so the earth was the first thing to come to the mind of the hearer when discussing the matter of resurrection, that is, the resurrection of the people of the graves.

Making the earth a resting-place includes an argument from the basic creation of the earth in a concise manner, and for this reason it was not dealt with further when the creation of the heavens was addressed.

﴿وَالْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا﴾

It is a conjunction ('aṭf) on ﴿the earth as a resting-place﴾ [al-Naba' 78:6]. So the wāw conjoins (al-jibāl) to (al-arḍ), and conjoins (awtādan) to (mihādan). This is an instance of conjoining two complements of a single governing word (ʿaṭf ʿalā maʿmūlayy ʿāmilin wāḥid). It occurs in eloquent speech and is permitted by the agreement of the grammarians, because the conjunctive particle takes the place of the governing word.

Awtād is the plural of watad, with a fatḥa on the wāw and a kasra on the tā' with two dots above. A watad is a thick stick, somewhat thicker than it is long, whose lower end is thinner than its upper end, which is driven into the ground to secure the ropes (aṭnāb) of a tent. A tent has many pegs according to the size of its circumference. Describing the mountains as pegs is an eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh), meaning: like pegs.

The reason the mountains are mentioned is that the mention of the earth prompted it, together with its comparison to a resting-place (mihād) that lies inside a house. Since a house is the kind of thing that comes to the hearer's mind on hearing "resting-place," the earth is treated as a house by way of implicit metaphor (makniyya). The mountains of the earth are then likened to the pegs of a house, as an imaginative evocation (takhyīl) of the earth, with its mountains, as a house with its resting-place and pegs.

Also, the abundance of mountains rising above the surface of the earth might suggest to minds that they do not fit with making the earth a resting-place. Hence, likening the mountains to pegs serves as a pleasing justification, like a fine excuse. It is therefore permissible for the mountains to be likened to pegs merely in appearance, together with this imaginative evocation, as in their saying: "I saw lions whose thicket is spears." It is also permissible for the mountains to be likened to the pegs of a tent in that they secure the tent from being uprooted by winds or shaken, on the basis that the creation of mountains for the earth contains a wisdom: to balance the earth's rotation within the atmospheric sphere. For the protrusion of mountains on the terrestrial globe causes them to break the current of the atmospheric sphere surrounding the earth, so that its current is balanced and the earth's movement within the air-sphere is not rapid.

Moreover, most of the earth's inhabitants, and the Arabs in particular, have abundant benefits from the mountains. Among them are the channels of valleys, the places where water settles at their foothills, the pastures for their livestock, their refuge in times of fear, and the lookout points over the roads leading to their homes when the enemy approaches them. For this reason the mention of the mountains has been frequent alongside the mention of the earth.

Thus the clause ﴿and the mountains as pegs﴾ is an interpolated insertion (idmāj muʿtariḍ) placed between the clause ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [al-Naba' 78:6] and the clause ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba' 78:8].

It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the affirmation (taqrir) in His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [An-Naba: 6]. The implied sense is: "And We created you in pairs." The affirmation here therefore retains its original form, since what is affirmed is the occurrence of the act of creation. For this reason He did not say, "Did We not create you in pairs?"

He used the verb "created" (khalaqa) rather than "made" (ja'ala) because it denotes the bringing into being of their very essences, and it is therefore more precise than "made."

The pronoun of address refers to the polytheists to whom the affirmation was directed in His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [An-Naba: 6]. This is an iltifat (shift) from the third-person narrative to the second-person address.

Although the verb it is coordinated with is in the present tense, the entry of (lam) upon it turns it into the past in meaning, since it is established that (lam) converts the meaning of the present tense into the past. For this reason it is appropriate to coordinate "We created you" with ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [An-Naba: 6] and ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ [An-Naba: 7]. All of these are an affirmation of something that has already occurred.

The verb was not put in the present tense like the verb it is coordinated with, because the present-tense form is used to evoke the image of the action as present to the mind, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿so it stirs up clouds﴾ [Ar-Rum: 48]. Thus the use of the present tense in ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [An-Naba: 6] indicates a summons to exercise reflection upon the creation of the earth and the mountains, since they are visible to them. Most observers, however, fail to reflect on their subtleties, because they have grown accustomed to seeing them since before the age of reflection. The ground beneath their feet is hardly something they look at, let alone reflect on its craftsmanship. As for the mountains, the effort of climbing them, of traversing their rugged terrain, of guarding their livestock from straying into their ravines, and of turning their gaze to the paths of the enemy when ascending their lookout points, all keep them from reflecting on how they were made. Therefore the present-tense verb was chosen, together with the mention of created things worthy of close contemplation and of drawing inference, so that their affirmation of what they were made to affirm would come with insight, and they would find no way to deny it.

The past-tense verb was used in ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ and what follows it, because the objects of the verb "We created" and of what is coordinated with it are not visible to them.

He mentioned among the created things that which is most closely connected with people, namely things whose states constantly present themselves to their perception. Their affirmation of these is therefore easier, since their indication is close to what is self-evident. He followed the inference from the creation of the earth and its mountains with an inference from the creation of people, so as to combine the affirmation of God's sole creatorship with an indication of the possibility of their resurrection. The proof in the creation of people concerns a great originative act, of which the second creation is of the same kind, and is therefore more feasible in the minds of those being argued with. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 21]. Owing to the connection we mentioned earlier regarding the beginning of the argument with the creation of the earth, it is that people come forth from the earth for resurrection. Likewise, the argument from the first creation of people is repeated, because they are the ones who will be recreated on the Day of Resurrection, and they are the ones who will come forth from the earth. To this meaning belongs His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And man says: "When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66] ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67].

"Pairs" (azwaj) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun of address in "We created you," because the intent is to argue from the creation of people and from the fact that people are in pairs. Since the verb "created" naturally takes the persons themselves as its object, its object was expressed as the pronoun for the persons. Since being in pairs naturally belongs to the manner of their existence, it was expressed as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun of address in "We created you." Had the verb been stated explicitly, it would have read: "We created you and made you pairs," in the manner of what preceded in His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ [An-Naba: 6], and of what comes later in His words: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ [An-Naba: 9].

"Azwaj" is the plural of zawj, which is a term for a number that repeats the unit once. It may be used as a descriptor, as the names of numbers are used, as in the verse of Labid:

"Until, when the two of them shed six Jumada months..."

The term zawj then came to be applied to each of a male and his female, whether human or animal. His saying "pairs" (azwaj) indicates that the male is a pair for the female and vice versa: the male is a pair for his female, and the female is a pair for her male. This was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿And We said: "O Adam, dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35], in the chapter of Al-Baqarah.

In His words: ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ there is an allusion to the wisdom in that creation, namely the bringing into being of the power of procreation through the union of male and female. This is the basis of the allusion to the argument for the possibility of restoring bodies, for He who is capable of originating this wondrous formation, beginning with the power of procreation, is capable of originating its like with the same precision or greater.

In it there is an argument for the great power and wisdom of God, and a favor upon people, in that He created them, and created them in a state that makes each of the two kinds suitable to be a pair for the other, so that cooperation and sharing in companionship and comfort may be realized. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made from it its mate that he might find rest in her﴾ [Al-A'raf: 189]. For this reason this affirmation was phrased by attaching the verb "created" to the pronoun for people, and making "pairs" a circumstantial qualifier of it, so that both considerations are gained together, rather than saying: "And We created for you pairs."

In this there is an urging upon them to give thanks by turning their attention to reflection upon what has been conveyed to them from God, who favored them with these blessings through the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It also contains an implicit rebuke: their turning away from accepting the Islamic call and their obstinacy regarding what has reached them of it is ingratitude for the blessing of the Bestower of blessings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 9:

﴿And We made your sleep a rest.﴾

He moved from the argument from the creation of people to the argument from their states, and he singled out from among them the state that is the strongest of their well-known states in resembling death, which is followed by resurrection. It is a recurring state, and they do not fail to feel the lesson in it, because the arrangement of the sleep system and what befalls it of wakefulness is the state most like the state of death and what follows it of resurrection.

The verb (ja'ala, "made") is preferred, because sleep is a condition for which the verb of making (ja'l) is appropriate, not the verb of creating (khalq), which is suited to essences, as came earlier in His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle?﴾ [An-Naba': 6]. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We made the night a garment, and We made the day a time for livelihood﴾ [An-Naba': 10].

The attribution of "sleep" to the pronoun of the addressees is not for restriction, to exclude the sleep of non-humans, since the sleep of every animal is a subat. Rather, the attribution serves to heighten the alert for the argument, meaning: the proof of resurrection is established and clear in the sleep which is among your states. Also, because describing it as subat contains a favour, and favour is specific to them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾ [Yunus: 67].

As for al-subat, with a dammah on the sin and a light ba': it is an infinitive-form noun with the meaning of al-sabt, that is, cutting off. That is, We made it for you a cutting-off of the body's work, such that the body must have it. Ibn al-A'rabi and Ibn Qutaybah pointed to this, for they took the meaning to be: "And We made your sleep a rest," so this is an explanation of meaning.

The word (subat) was preferred because of what it carries of the notion of cutting off from work, to correspond to His saying after it: ﴿And We made the day a time for livelihood﴾ [An-Naba': 11], as will come.
Subat is also applied to light sleep, but that is not intended in this verse, since it would not be sound for the meaning to be: "And We made your sleep a sleep, nor a light sleep."

In Al-Razi's commentary: some of the heretics criticised this verse and said: subat is sleep, so the meaning is: "And We made your sleep a sleep." He went on to interpret it with three views from the exegetes, of which only what Ibn al-A'rabi said is sound, that subat is cutting off, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who is a god other than Allah that would bring you a night wherein you may rest?﴾ [Al-Qasas: 72], and this is the original meaning of the derivatives of the root s-b-t.

Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Sidah denied that the verb sabata means "to rest," that is, it is not the meaning of the word; so whoever explains subat as rest intends an explanation of the resulting meaning.

In this there is a favour upon people, by the creation of the system of sleep in them, so that they may obtain rest from the fatigue of the work for which they toil in their day. Allah, exalted is He, made sleep arise in the human without his choice, for sleep compels the human to cease work so that rest may be attained for his nervous system whose pillar is in the brain. By that rest the nerve renews the powers that the work of the senses and the movements and actions of the limbs have weakened, such that if someone's desire is set on staying awake, sleep must overcome him. That is a kindness to the human, so that what benefits his faculties comes to him by compulsion upon him, lest he neglect it. For this reason it is said: the people who sleep least are the shortest-lived, and so too are animals.

﴿And We made the night a garment﴾.

This completes the argument that precedes it and the favour contained in it. The night being a garment is a condition that prepares and suits sleep, and helps one to enjoy its rest and benefit from it. The night is a darkness that comes over the atmosphere when the sunlight is withdrawn from a part of the earth's sphere. With that darkness, visible things are hidden from sight, so walking, work and occupation become difficult, and activity declines. The nerves then become ready for slackening, and sleep overtakes them, and rest (subat) results from these wondrous preliminaries. Therefore the arrangement of the night is a sign of God Most High's sole act of creation and the wondrous measure of His decree.

It is also evidence that the restoration of bodies after their annihilation is not impossible for Him, Most High. Had the deniers reflected on it, they would have known that God is capable of resurrection. But when they denied the Messenger's (ﷺ) report of it, and in this there is a favour upon them through this arrangement, in which lies His gentleness towards them and the ease of their lives, had they measured it by its true measure, they would have given thanks and not associated partners. So the state of the night came quickly to mind when the state of sleep was mentioned, and mentioning sleep became an occasion for moving to the argument from the state of the night, in accordance with the understanding of the listeners.

The meaning of making the night a garment revolves around describing a particular state belonging to the night, expressed by the word "garment."

It is permissible for the garment to be understood in its nominal sense, which is its most common usage, namely what a person wears of clothing. Then the description of the night by it would be on the presumption of a comparative particle (kaf al-tashbih), in the manner of the eloquent simile: We made the night for the human being like a garment for him. The point of resemblance may be covering, and under it are three meanings:

The first: the night conceals the human being just as a garment conceals him. A person in the night secludes himself with his affairs which he does not commit in the daytime, because he does not like the eyes to see them. In this there is an allusion to refuting a principle of the Dahriyya (materialists), that the night is the lord of darkness. This is the doctrine of the Magians (Majus), who believe that all created things are made from two origins, that is, two gods: the god of light, who is the author of good, and the god of darkness, who is the author of evil. They are called the Dualists (Thanawiyya) because they affirmed two gods. They are groups of differing doctrines regarding how the world came into being from those two origins. The most famous of these groups is one called the Manichaeans (Maniyya), named after a man called (Mani), a Persian before Islam. Another is called the Mazdakites (Mazdakiyya), named after a man called (Mazdak), a Persian before Islam. Abu al-Tayyib took the meaning of this allusion in his saying:

"How many a favour the darkness of night has done you,
Tells that the Manichaeans lie."

The second of the two meanings of the point of resemblance with a garment: it is the similarity in being gentle to the one who wears it and suitable to his comfort. Since the night is a rest for the human being, and since it encompasses all his senses and nerves, it was likened to a garment in that respect. The general sense of this meaning is attributed to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Qatada, since they interpreted (subatan) as "rest."

The third meaning: the point of resemblance with a garment is protection. The night protects the human being from dangers and from being attacked. The Arabs would not raid one another at night; raids only took place in the morning. For this reason, when a people was raided, a man would cry out to his tribe, saying: "Ya sabahaah!" (Alas, morning!). It is said: "The enemy raided them at dawn." When they set a watch on the hills, a lookout (nazura) against what enemies might come upon them, they would post it by day, and when the night darkened, the watch would descend. As Labid said, recalling that and recalling his horse:

"Until, when its darkness cast a hand upon a disbeliever,
and concealed the nakedness of the frontier posts,
I dismounted, and it stood erect like a tall trunk,
smooth, whose cutters are kept from it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 11:

﴿And We made the day a time for livelihood.﴾

When the creation of the system of the night was mentioned, it was paired with the creation of the system of the day. Al-nahar (the day) is the time in which the light of the sun spreads over a large part of the terrestrial sphere. In it there is a lesson in the precision of the making and its perfection, for two systems were made, of differing origins, namely the shining of the sun's light and its concealment above the earth. These are two blessings for mankind, differing in their causes and effects: the blessing of the night returns to rest and tranquility, and the blessing of the day returns to work and striving, because the day follows the night, so that a person has renewed his rest, regained his vigor, and is able to undertake various works through seeing persons and roads.

Since most work takes place during the day for the sake of livelihood (ma'ash), the day is described as ma'ash. The mention of the day after the mention of both sleep and night has the implication that the day is the beginning of the time of wakefulness, which is the opposite of sleep. Thus their contrast with the day becomes, in estimation: "And We made the day and wakefulness within it a livelihood," so the speech contains an elision (ikhtiba') indicated by the contrast. Through this, there occur between the three clauses two instances of antithesis (mutabaqa), among the rhetorical embellishments (muhassinat badi'iyya), both verbally and implicitly.

Al-ma'ash: it is used as a verbal noun of 'ash, when one is alive, so al-ma'ash means life; and it is used as a noun for that by which a person subsists, such as food and drink, not according to a rule of derivation.

Both meanings are suitable for the verse. The meaning may be: "And We made the day a life for you," the wakefulness in it being likened to life. Or the meaning may be: "And We made the day a means of subsistence for you," and describing it as a means of subsistence is also a metaphor (majaz) by the relation of causation ( 'alaqat al-sababiyya), because the day is a cause of work, which is the cause of obtaining livelihood. This corresponds to the making of the night as subat (rest), in the sense of cessation from work. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73].

Thus, in the contrast of subat (rest) with ma'ash (livelihood) on these two considerations, there are two antitheses among the rhetorical embellishments.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 12:

﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens].﴾

It is fitting, after mentioning the night and the day, which are among the manifestations of the horizon called "sky" (sama'), that this be followed, along with what preceded it of the creation of the lower world, by mention of the creation of the upper worlds.

Al-bina' (construction): the making by a maker, or the fashioning by a craftsman, of a house or palace of stone and clay, or of cloth, or of hide, upon the face of the earth. It is the verbal noun of banaa (to build). Thus a house of clay is mabni (built), and a tent is mabniyya (built), and the tent-pole and the dome of hide are both mabniyyan (built). Construction necessarily entails raising something above the earth, so digging is not construction, nor is hewing rocks out of mountains construction. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose supports are mightiest and tallest."

Here he mentioned the supports (da'a'im), which are parts of the tent.

The verb "built" (banayna) in this verse is used figuratively to mean: We created that which is high above people, because its being created high resembles building.

Accordingly, His saying "above you" (fawqakum) is an indication of the aspect of resemblance in the application of the verb "built" to it. This is not a stripping away (tajrid) of the metaphor, because height is not specific to built things, and it also serves to alert souls to reflect and contemplate those seven strong [heavens].

The "seven strong" are the heavens, so this is the mention of the attribute with the omission of the qualified noun, known from context, as in His exalted saying: ﴿We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. For this reason the attribute came with the feminine numeral; the implied phrase is "seven heavens."

It is permissible that by "the seven" is meant the seven well-known planets among people at that time, namely: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. This is their order according to the height of some above others, as indicated by the eclipse of some by others when one comes between it and the light of the Sun, from which the rest of the planets acquire their light from the Sun's rays.

This interpretation is the most apparent, because the lesson drawn from it is more evident, since those addressed do not see the seven heavens, but they see these wandering bodies and are familiar with them, unlike other wandering bodies later discovered by astronomers, namely Saturn (Sitwrn), Neptune (Nibtun) and Uranus (Awrānūs). These are, in God's knowledge, undoubtedly [part of creation], according to His saying: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14], and because God says only what is true and sincere, and He brings meanings close to people in proportion to their understanding, out of mercy toward them.

As for the earth, it was recently counted among the wandering planets, and the Moon was omitted from the planets to show that its motion follows the motion of the earth. However, this has no bearing on the argument, because the argument rests on what was known and accepted at that time, and all of it is the handiwork of God.

It is also permissible that by the seven heavens are meant seven upper layers which God alone knows, and people have been convinced since antiquity that they are seven heavens.

Shidad (strong) is the plural of shadida, the feminine of one described by strength, and shidda means power.

The meaning: they are firm in their creation, strong in their bodies, their affairs do not fall into disorder, and they do not diminish over the passage of time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 13:

﴿And We have made a blazing lamp.﴾

The mention of the heavens is accompanied by the mention of the greatest thing that people observe in their expanse, namely the sun. In this, along with the lesson in its creation, there is a lesson in its being in that attribute, and a favour upon people through their benefiting from its light in many ways.

Page 24

Al-siraj (lamp): its literal meaning is the lamp (misbah) by which one is illuminated. It is a vessel in which oil is placed, and in the oil is a twisted wick called al-dhubala, which is lit with fire and gives light as long as the oil remains moist in it.

The discussion concerns the eloquent metaphor (al-tashbih al-baligh), and the purpose of the metaphor is to bring the attribute of the thing compared (al-mushabbah) closer to the minds, as was previously mentioned in Surat Nuh.

This closeness is increased by describing the lamp as wahhaj, i.e., intensely bright.

Al-wahhaj: its root meaning is that which has intense wahaj (with a fatha on the waw and a fatha on the ha; it is also said with a fatha on the waw and a sukun on the ha), which is blazing. It is said: "the fire wahajat" when it blazed with intense burning.

Al-wahhaj is also applied to that which is shining and luminous, and this is the meaning intended here, because the description wahhaj is applied to siraj, meaning a lamp of intense illumination. One does not say siraj multahib (a flaming lamp).

Al-Raghib said: al-wahaj is the occurrence of light and heat from fire. In al-Asas, the saying "siraj wahhaj" is counted under the literal (haqiqa) category. In accordance with this, al-Kashshaf's statement runs: "gleaming and blazing, and the fire tawahhajat when it flared up, so it shone with its light and heat." Therefore, the expression of the sun as a lamp in this verse is the place of the metaphor.

For this reason the verb (ja'alna, "We made") was preferred over (khalaqna, "We created"), because its being a blazing lamp is a state of its states, and the verb of creation is only attached to essences.

So the meaning is: "And We made for you a blazing lamp," or "And We made in the seven solid heavens a blazing lamp," in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh: 15] ﴿and made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16], and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾ [al-Furqan: 61], whether you take the pronoun in (fiha) as referring to "the sky" or to "the constellations," since the constellations are the constellations of the sky.

His saying "siraj" is a noun of genus (ism jins); it may be intended as one individual of that genus, so it is possible that the sun or the moon is intended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 14–17:

﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth,﴾ ﴿that We might bring forth thereby grain and plants,﴾ ﴿and gardens of thick foliage.﴾

This is an argument from another of the conditions which God Most High has placed in the order of existing things, and made it a source resembling life after something resembling death, or near to it, and a source for the coming into being of existing things from fine particles. This condition is the sending down of rainwater from the clouds onto the earth, whereupon the earth brings forth by it ears of grain, trees and herbage. All of these have a life close to the life of man and animal, namely the life of growth. Thus this becomes evidence for people of the state of resurrection after death, by way of an argument from analogy that indicates its possibility, until the doubts of those who deny the impossibility of resurrection vanish from their souls.

This which is pointed out here has been stated explicitly in several places of the Qur'an, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain of harvest﴾ [Qaf: 9] ﴿and tall palm trees with ranged spathes﴾ [Qaf: 10] ﴿as provision for the servants; and We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11]. In the verse there are thus two arguments: from the sending down of water from the clouds, and from the growing of plants. In this there is also a favour upon those who turn away from reflecting on the signs of God's craftsmanship, which are incentives to thank the Benefactor for them, because of the benefits they contain for people in their provision and the provision of their livestock, and in their enjoyment and the beauty of their sights. For if they thanked the Benefactor for them, they would be—when it reaches them from Him that He calls them to reflect on the proofs—prepared for reflection, expecting that the call addressed to them is true in its attribution to God, and so the indication would not be hidden from them.

The transition from mention of the heavens to mention of the clouds and rain is strong.

Al-Mu'sirat (المُعْصِراتِ): with a damma on the mim and a kasra on the sad, the clouds that carry rainwater; its singular is mu'sirah, an active participle, from a'sarat al-sahabah when it is time for it to press, i.e., to release a release resembling pressing. So the hamza of (a'sara) indicates the sense of approaching readiness (al-hayn-unah), which is an attested usage, and is called the hamzat al-tahay'ah (the hamza of preparation), as in their saying: ajazza al-zar'u, when it is time for it to be reaped (with a zay at its end), and ahsada when the time of its harvest has come. It appears from the words of the author of al-Kashshaf that the hamza of approaching readiness indicates the sense of readiness to receive the action, and also indicates the sense of readiness to issue the action, for he mentioned: a'sarat al-jariyah, i.e., the time came for her to begin menstruating. Ibn Qutaybah in Adab al-Katib mentioned: arkaba al-muhr, when it was time for it to be ridden, and aqtafa al-karm, when it was time for it to be plucked. Then he mentioned: aqtafa al-qawm: the time came for them to pluck their vines, and antajat al-khayl: the time came for their foaling.

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah, at his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that God drives the clouds﴾ [al-Nur: 43] and the verse of Surah al-Nur, the Arabs say: when God Most High makes the clouds heaped up, He brings the wind, which presses some of them against others, so the rain (al-wadq) comes out of them. From this is His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth﴾. From this also is the verse of Hassan:

Both of them have milked the juice, so hand me a cup whose two were the loosest at the joint.

Hassan meant wine and the water with which it was mixed; i.e., this is from the juice of the grape, and this is from the juice of the cloud. The judge of Basra, Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-'Anbari, explained this interpretation to the people whose companion had sworn by divorce that he would ask the judge about the interpretation of Hassan's verse. End quote.

Al-Thajjaj: that which pours out with force; it is fa'alul from thajja (intransitive) when it pours out. It is said: thajja al-ma', when water pours out with force, so it is an intransitive verb. The verb thajj may also be attributed to the cloud, it is said: thajja al-sahab yathujju (with a damma on the tha), when it pours out water, and then it is a transitive verb.

The description of the water here as thajjaj is for the sake of favour (al-imtinan).

The wisdom of sending rain down from the clouds has been explained: that God made it for the growth of plants from the earth, combining favour with an allusion to the argument for the nearness of resurrection, so that their acknowledgment of resurrection and thanks to the Maker may be attained.

The verb (li-nukhrija) was used instead of something like li-nunbita, because the intended aim is an allusion to depicting the manner of the resurrection of people from the earth, since that is the primary purpose of this speech. Do you not see that when the primary purpose of the verse in Surah Qaf was favour, the verb (anbatna) was used in His saying:

﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and caused to grow thereby gardens﴾ [Qaf: 9], and the verse following, then it was secondarily followed by the argument from it for resurrection, in His saying: ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11]. Resurrection is an emergence from the earth. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And from it We bring you out a second time﴾ [Ta-Ha: 55] in Surah Ta-Ha.

Al-habb: a collective noun whose singular is habbah, which is a seed. What is meant by habb here is the grain eaten by people, such as wheat, barley, spelt, maize, rice, and pulses, which are the grains that are the fruit of ears and the like.

Al-nabat: originally a verbal noun of nabata al-zar'u (the crop grew). He, Exalted, said: ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Nabat was applied to the one that grows, from the application of the verbal noun to the agent, originally intensive, then its use became common and the intensiveness was forgotten.

What is meant by it here is the plant whose seed is not eaten but which is benefited from in itself, namely what cattle and beasts eat, such as chaff, clover, alfalfa, grass, and other things.

The gardens (jannat) have been made the object of (nukhrija) under an implied genitive, i.e., palms of gardens or trees of gardens, because jannat is the plural of jannah, which is a piece of land planted with palms, or palms and vines, or with all fruit-bearing trees, such as figs and pomegranates, as occurs in several places of the Qur'an, and these are varied usages according to the differences of the places of growth.

The reason for preferring the word jannat is that it contains an allusion to the completion of the favour, because they loved gardens and orchards for the enjoyment they contain of shade, fruits, water, and beauty of view. For this reason it was followed by the description alfaf, since it increases its beauty. Although our farmers prefer spacing between trees because that is more abundant in quantity of fruit, since their distance is more beneficial to them through the passage of air and sunlight, nonetheless the context of the verse here is favour with what contains the delight of people.

Alfaf: a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like awza' and akhyaf, i.e., every garden is densely interwoven, that is, its trees are intertwined with one another.

The description of the garden as alfaf is based on metaphor in the predicate (al-majaz al-'aqli), because the interweaving is in its trees, but since the trees do not usually intertwine with one another unless a garden gathers them,

alfaf was attributed to jannat by way of description, and perhaps it is one of the innovations of the Qur'an, since I have not seen evidence for it from the speech of the Arabs before the Qur'an.

It is said: alfaf is the plural of lif (with a kasra on the lam), on the pattern of jidh', i.e., every garden of them is lif (with a kasra on the lam), but they did not cite evidence for it. It is mentioned in al-Kashshaf that the author of al-Iqlid mentioned a verse recited by al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Tusi, and did not attribute it to a speaker. In al-Kashshaf it is claimed that Ibn Qutaybah supposed it to be laffa'  and luff, then alfaf (i.e., alfaf is a plural of plural), and said: I do not think he finds a parallel for it. That is, a form fu'l is not pluralized into af'al, i.e., there is no parallel to it, since one does not say khudr and akhdar, or humr and ahmar. He means that the eloquent speech does not come out in a usage whose parallel has not been established in the speech of the Arabs, although there is an interpretation of it in a valid way.

So the most apparent of the views is that alfaf is a collective noun with no singular from its own form.

With this argument and favour the proofs that were set forth for them concerning God Most High's singularity in divinity are concluded, and they include an allusion to the possibility of resurrection, and what favours upon them were embedded within them, perhaps they will remember the blessing and feel the obligation to thank the Benefactor, and not find it monstrous to nullify associates in divinity, and consider what has reached them from Him concerning the report of resurrection and recompense, so that they direct their minds to reflect on the proofs of the truth of that.

These proofs began with the proofs of the creation of the earth and its condition, and reminder roamed with them over the most important things on the earth of inanimate matter and animals, then what is on the horizon of the accidents of night and day, then the wandering with reflection rose up with them to the creation of the heavens, especially the sun, then it descended with them to the proofs of the clouds and rain, so they descended with it to what comes out of the earth of wondrous crafts and the furthest benefits, and then they look from whence they set out, and this is from the return of the last to the first.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾ [An-Naba': 17] ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾.

This is an explanation of what was stated in summary by His saying: ﴿about the great news﴾ [An-Naba': 2] ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾ [An-Naba': 3]. It is the purpose intended by the context of the opening (al-fatihah) with which the surah began, and the mention of bringing forth in His saying: ﴿So that We may bring forth thereby grain and plants﴾ [An-Naba': 15] etc. prepared the transition, because that was compared to the bringing forth of human bodies for resurrection, as the Exalted said: ﴿So We caused to grow thereby gardens and grain of harvest﴾ [Qaf: 9], up to His saying: ﴿Thus is the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11] in Surah Qaf.

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani) that follows His saying: ﴿So that We may bring forth thereby grain and plants﴾ [An-Naba': 15] and the verse, in what it intends by way of indicating the proof of resurrection.

The statement is emphasized with the particle of emphasis, because in it is a refutation of the denial and rejection of the polytheists concerning the Day of Decision.

The Day of Decision (yawm al-fasl) is the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

Al-fasl (decision) is distinguishing between mixed things. Its use became common for distinguishing between meanings that are similar and ambiguous; therefore it was applied to judgment, and it may be added to, so one says: fasl al-qada' (the decisiveness of judgment), i.e., a kind of separation, because judgment distinguishes truth from injustice.

So recompense for deeds is a separation between people, some from others.

The expression "the Day of Decision" was chosen for two matters: First, that it is a distinction between the establishment of what they denied, namely resurrection and recompense, and that is a separation between truth and their falsehood.

Second, the judgment between people concerning what they disagreed about, and what some of them transgressed against others.

The insertion of the verb (kana) is to convey that its appointed time is rooted in the knowledge of God, according to what His wisdom, which He alone knows best, requires, and that their urgency for it does not bring it forward from its appointed time.

Page 30
The phrase "the Day of Decision" has come up more than once, the last of which was in Surah al-Mursalat.
The description of the Qur'an as decisive (fasl) comes in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [At-Tariq: 13] in Surah At-Tariq.

Al-miqat (appointed time) is a noun of the pattern mif'al derived from al-waqt (time). Al-waqt is the specified time for a task, and for this reason the word waqt is not used except restricted by an addition or the like, such as: waqt al-salah (the time of prayer).

So miqat is formed on the pattern of an instrument noun, but what is meant by it is the very time specified for something, like mi'ad and milad, departing from being a noun of instrument to being a noun for the very thing from which it is derived. The context indicates the object of miqat, i.e., it was an appointed time for resurrection and recompense.

So its being a miqat is an allusive metonymy (kinayah talwihiyyah) for the certainty of its occurrence, since appointing a time is only for a time whose occurrence is certain, even if it is delayed and slow.

This is a response to their question about hastening it and about the reason for its delay, a question by which they intended mockery of its report.

The meaning: the delay of its occurrence does not indicate the negation of its taking place.

The meaning: your denial of it is not something that compels us to change its specified season, but God is granting you respite for a period.

In this is a warning to them that it is not known; perhaps it will occur soon. The Exalted said: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [Al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Say: perhaps it will be near﴾ [Al-Isra': 51].

﴿The Day the Horn is blown﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (yawm al-fasl).

The word (yawm) is annexed to the clause ﴿is blown in the Horn﴾, so (yawm) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its fatha is a case-marking fatha, because it is annexed to a clause whose first word is inflected, namely the present-tense verb.

The benefit of this substitution is the detailing of some states of the Decision and some terrors of the Day of Decision.

Al-sur: the trumpet. It is a horn of an ox, hollow in its middle, with part of its hollow narrowed, and it is made of wood or of copper; the blower blows into it and the sound comes out strong, to call people to gather. What is most often called with it is the army and the scattered crowds, so that they gather for a task the commander who orders the blowing intends.

The verb (yunfakh) is built for the passive (with the deputy of the agent) because the purpose does not depend on knowing the one who blows; rather, the purpose is knowing this great event and the manner of its occurrence.

The blowing into the Horn may be a figure for the manner of calling people and gathering them to the assembly, in the manner of an army scattered for rest, or pursuit of an enemy, who soon gather at the place of their commander.

It may also be a blowing by which revival occurs, whose nature is not known, since the states of the Hereafter are not like the states of this world; so this blowing is expressed as a matter of special creation, namely the creation of bodies after their decay and the infusion of their spirits into their remains. It is reported in traditions that the angel assigned to this blowing is Israfil, and this has been mentioned more than once before.

The conjunction of (ta'tuna) with the fa' indicates that the blowing is followed by their coming to the reckoning.

Al-ityan: presence at a place to which one who walks proceeds; so al-ityan is attainment.

The omission of what occurs between the blowing into the Horn and their presence is to increase the notification of the swiftness of the coming about of the arrival, so that it is as if it occurs at the blowing: "then you live, then you move, then you come."

(Afwaajan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in (ta'tuna). Afwaj is the plural of fawj, with fa' vowelled and waw sukun. A fawj is a group of companions of people divided by differences of aims, so nations will be afwaj, and the righteous and others will be afwaj. The Exalted said: ﴿Whenever a company is thrown into it, its keepers will ask them﴾ [Al-Mulk: 8], etc.

The meaning: you will come divided into groups and companies, and this division is according to states, like believers and disbelievers, and all of those are categories and ranks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 19:

[Page 32]
﴿And the sky will be opened, and it will become gates.﴾
This clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in (ta'tūna, "you come").

The implied sense is: "and the sky has been opened," meaning the blowing (of the Trumpet) has already occurred before that or together with it.

It is also permissible for it to be coordinated (ma'tufa) with the clause ﴿The Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Naba': 18], in which case "yawm" (the day) is considered as being in construction (mudaf) with this clause, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. The use of the past tense verb in this way is to affirm the occurrence of this opening, as though its occurrence has already passed.

The opening of the sky (fath al-sama') is its splitting open by the descent of the angels from some of the heavens, which are their dwelling place, a descent by which they attend to carry out the command of recompense, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25], ﴿The sovereignty that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (wa-futtiḥat) with the doubled tā' (tashdid), and this is an intensification of the act of opening, by its abundance or its severity, indicating that it is a great opening, because splitting the sky is something only God is able to do.

'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the single tā' (takhfif), in accordance with the original form of the verb, and the mere attachment of the opening to the sky indicates that it is a severe opening.

In the opening there is a lesson, because the heavens were once joined together; when their joining is corrupted and they are pierced with openings, the order of the transient world is disrupted with it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1] up to His saying: ﴿O man, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6].

So the tafattuh (repeated opening) and the fath (opening) are the same in the intended meaning, which is the terrifying of the Day of Judgment.

Following the opening of the sky, with the particle of sequence (fa'), comes: ﴿so it becomes gates﴾, that is, possessing gates.

So His saying "gates" (abwāban) is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning "like gates." At that point there is no barrier remaining between the inhabitants of the heavens and the people, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4].

[Page 33]
The statement about the sky that it is "gates" follows the manner of exaggeration in description, as though it were itself gates, to indicate the abundance of openings within it. Close to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], where the gushing is attributed to the word "earth" and the noun "springs" is brought as a specification (tamyiz). This suits the meaning of the doubled-tā' reading and confirms it, and it restricts and clarifies the meaning of the single-tā' reading.

And (kānat) here means: became.

The meaning of becoming (al-sayrūrah) is among the meanings of kāna and its four sisters, which are: zalla, bāta, amsā and aṣbaḥa. The indication of this is that it is a consequence (mufarra') of (futtiḥat), and its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the sky is split open and becomes rose-red like oil dregs﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

The "abwāb" (gates) is the plural of bāb, which is the opening through which one enters in a barrier of a wall, a fence, a screen or a tent. It was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they closed the doors﴾ [Yusuf: 23] in Surat Yusuf, and in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 20:

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, so they will be a mirage.﴾

Al-taysir (setting in motion): making a thing move, i.e., walking. Here it is applied to removal from its place: the mountains are carried away and uprooted from their settled places swiftly, through earthquakes or the like, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day the earth and the mountains will quake, and the mountains will become heaps of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], until it is as though they are moving from one place to another. This is a removal accompanied by crumbling, as indicated by its being followed by His saying: ﴿so they will be a mirage﴾, because the apparent sense of "following" is that no delay accompanies it, i.e., they become like a mirage in that they are nothing.

The discussion of the passive form in (suyyirat) is like the discussion of ﴿And the sky will be opened﴾ [al-Naba: 19].

Likewise His saying: ﴿so they will be a mirage﴾ is like His saying: ﴿so it will be gates﴾ [al-Naba: 19].

Al-sarab (mirage): what appears in the deserts resembling water but is not water; rather it is a condition in the near atmosphere that arises from the accumulation of vapors on the surface of the earth. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He:

Page 34
﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [al-Nur: 39] in Surat al-Nur.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verses 21–23:

﴿Indeed, Hell has always been a lookout post,﴾ ﴿a dwelling place for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿remaining in it for ages.﴾

It is permissible that the clause ﴿Indeed, Hell has always been a lookout post﴾ is in the position of a second predicate (khabar thani) of (inna) from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision has always been an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba' 17]. The implied construction is: "Indeed, the Day of Decision, indeed Hell has been a lookout post in it for the transgressors." The returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted, and it is indicated by His saying (mirsadan), meaning "a lookout post in it," that is, on that Day. This is because the meaning of mirsad (lookout post) is close to the meaning of miqat (appointed time), since both determine the recompense of the transgressors.

The entry of the particle (inna) on the predicate of (inna) gives a further emphasis upon the emphasis conveyed by the emphatic particle that enters upon His saying "the Day of Decision," in the manner of the saying of Jarir:

"Indeed the Caliph, indeed God has clothed him
With the garment of sovereignty, by which the rings are made to move."

From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners, indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj 17], as has preceded in Surat al-Hajj. The clause is a continuation of what they were addressed with in His saying: ﴿The Day the Trumpet is blown, and you come forth in throngs﴾ [al-Naba' 18].

The expression "the transgressors" (al-taghin) is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, for the purpose of recording upon them the attribute of transgression. This is because the expected form would be to say "for you a place of return."

It is also permissible that the clause is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) in response to the clause ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision has always been an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba' 17] and what follows it. This is because such matters arouse in the souls of the listeners a desire to know what will happen after those terrors. So it is answered with the content of ﴿Indeed, Hell has always been a lookout post﴾, the verse. Accordingly, there is in His saying "for the transgressors" no deviation from what the apparent construction requires.

Hell is mentioned first because the context is one of threat, since the surah began with mention of the denial of resurrection by the polytheists, and for the reason that we will mention regarding the arrangement of these clauses.

[p. 35]

Jahannam (Hell) is the name of the abode of punishment in the Hereafter. It is said that it is an arabicized word (mu'arrab), so it is possibly arabicized from Hebrew or from another Semitic language. It was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿Hell is enough for him, and what an evil resting place﴾ [al-Baqarah 206], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-mirsad (lookout post) is the place of watching (al-rasd), that is, observation (al-raqaba). It is of the pattern mif'al, which is predominantly used for the instrument of an action, like midmar (a place where horses are trained) and minhaj (a path or place from which one proceeds).

The meaning is: Hell is a place from which those appointed over it watch and await whoever is driven toward it from among the people of transgression, just as the people of a lookout post await whoever comes to them from an enemy.

It is also permissible that mirsad is a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern mif'al, meaning rasd (watching). Describing Hell with it is for emphasis, as though it were the very origin of watching, that is, it lets none escape of those upon whom entry into it is decreed.

It is also permissible that mirsad is on the pattern of an intensive form (ziyat mubalagha) for one who watches intensively, like the attributes migyar and mi'tar. Hell is described with it by way of metaphor (isti'ara), and the feminine marker (ha') was not attached to it, because Hell was likened to a single individual of the watchers (rasad, with the sad vowelled), namely one of the guards who stands at the lookout post, since the guard is only a man.

The complement of mirsadan is omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿for the transgressors a place of return﴾. The implied construction is: "a lookout post for the transgressors." This is better, because the rhyming units (qara'in) of the surah are short, so it is good to pause at "mirsadan" so that it serves as a rhyme.

You may make "for the transgressors" dependent on "mirsadan" and make the complement of "ma'aban" an implied element indicated by "for the transgressors." This would be like the enjambment (tadmin) in poetry, since it carries over a remainder of what was in the first rhyme into the following rhyme, so the rhyme becomes long.

If you wish to make "for the transgressors" a word contested between "mirsadan" and "ma'aban," there is no objection to that in meaning.

The verb "kanat" (has been) was inserted instead of saying "indeed Hell is a lookout post," to indicate that making it a lookout post is a matter decreed for it, as has preceded in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision has always been an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba' 17]. In this there is an indication of the vastness of God's knowledge, the Exalted, since He prepared punishment for the transgressors in His eternity.

[p. 36]

Ma'aban (a place of return): it is the place of return (al-awb), which is going back. It was applied to the place of settling and dwelling by an application whose origin is a metaphor (kinaya), and then its usage became common, so it became a noun for the place where a person settles.

"Ma'aban" is in the accusative either as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "Jahannam," or as a second predicate of the verb "kanat," or as a substitutive of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from "mirsadan," because the lookout post includes matters intended, among them that they will go to Hell.

"Lil-taghin" (for the transgressors) is the complement of "ma'aban," and it was placed before it in order to induce terror in the polytheists, who by their polytheism transgressed against God. This is better, as you have understood just now. You may also make it dependent on "mirsadan," or a word contested between "mirsadan" and "ma'aban," as you have understood just now.

Al-tughyan (transgression) is going beyond the limit in disregarding the rights of others and in arrogance. The definite article in it is for a prior reference (al-'ahd), so what is meant by it are the polytheists addressed in His saying: ﴿and you come forth in throngs﴾ [al-Naba' 18]. It is therefore an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, for the purpose of indicating the cause for which Hell was made theirs, because associating partners with God is the utmost transgression. The polytheists turned away from His worship, and were arrogant toward His Messenger (ﷺ), refusing to accept his call.
