Bard (coolness) is the opposite of heat, and it is a relief for those whose torment is heat, i.e., they will not be given relief by a cool breeze, and coolness is the most delightful thing sought by one who is scorched by heat. From Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu 'Ubaydah and a small group, the interpretation of bard is sleep, and they cited two verses of poetry that are not clear in their meaning. In any case, reading the verse in this sense is a forced reading for which there is no need, and the conjunction ﴿wa-lā sharāban﴾ contradicts it. Sharab is what is drunk, and what is meant by it is the water that removes thirst. Ḥamīm (boiling water) is water of extreme heat.

صفحة ٣٨
Ghassaq: Al-Jumhur read it with a light sīn, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with a doubled sīn; both are two dialectal forms of it. Its meaning is the pus that flows from the wounds of burning, which is also al-muhl, and both were discussed in Surah Sad.

The exception ﴿ḥamīman wa-ghassaqan﴾ is from (bardan) or (sharaban) by way of the ordered laff wa-nashr (wrapping and spreading), and it is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), because ḥamīm is not of the same kind as coolness at all, since it is intensely hot, and because ghassaq is not of the same kind as drink, since al-muhl is not of the same kind as drink.

The meaning is: they will taste the ḥamīm, as it is poured over their bodies, and the ghassaq, as it flows over the places of burning, increasing their pain.

The form of the exception here is the affirmation of a thing by something resembling its opposite in appearance.

(Jaza'an) is accusative as a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun of (yadhūqūna), meaning: that being the state of recompense, i.e., they are repaid with it. Thus the circumstantial phrase here is a verbal noun interpreted in the sense of a descriptive attribute, and it is more eloquent than a plain attribute.

Wifāq is the verbal noun of wāfaqa, interpreted as a descriptive attribute, meaning: in agreement with the deed for which they are repaid, which is denial of the Resurrection and denial of the Qur'an, as indicated by the reason given after it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾ [al-Naba': 27] ﴿and they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾ [al-Naba': 28].

For that is the root of their persistence in disbelief, and these are two roots: one negative, which is the denial of the Resurrection, and the other positive, which is their attributing to the Messenger ﷺ and the Qur'an falsehood. So they were punished for the negative root with a negative punishment, which is their deprivation of coolness and drink, and for the positive root with a positive recompense, which is the ḥamīm poured over their bodies and the ghassaq passing over their wounds.

﴿Indeed, they used not to hope for a reckoning﴾ ﴿and they denied Our signs with [utter] denial.﴾ The placement of this sentence is that of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿Indeed, Hell has been an ambush﴾ [An-Naba': 21] up to His words ﴿a recompense in full accord﴾ [An-Naba': 26]. For this reason it is detached (fusilat) from what precedes it.

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed they﴾ refers back to the tyrants (al-taghun).

The particle ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) here serves to emphasise the predicate (li'l-ihtimam bi'l-khabar) and is not meant to rebut a denial, since no one denies that they do not hope for a reckoning and that they deny the Qur'an. When the particle inna is intended merely for emphasis, it takes the place of the connecting fa' (fa' al-tafri'), conveying causation. This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 32] and His words ﴿Indeed, the cow has become confused for us﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 70] in Surat al-Baqarah. Accordingly, the sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida) between what precedes it and the sentence ﴿So taste [it]﴾ [An-Naba': 30].

You already know the appropriateness of their recompense to their crime, from His words just above, ﴿a recompense in full accord﴾ [An-Naba': 26], which further clarifies the aspect of causation.

His words ﴿they do not hope for a reckoning﴾ are a negation of their hope that the recompense would occur.

The word raja' (hope) is well known for anticipating a desired matter, whereas reckoning is not something good for them, such that the negation of their anticipating it could be treated as a negation of hope. Thus the apparent expectation would have been to express their anticipation with the root tawaqqu' (expectation), which is anticipation of a disliked matter. It therefore becomes clear that the reason for shifting from the root tawaqqu' to the root raja' is this: when God related the recompense and punishment of the tyrants, the Muslims received that with joy, knowing that they would be saved from what the tyrants would encounter, so they were awaiting the Day of Reckoning with the anticipation of hope. Thus the negation of the hope for the Day of Reckoning from the polytheists comprises, by its explicit meaning, their non-belief in its occurrence, and by its implicit meaning (kinaya) the hope of the believers in its occurrence, through the mode of allusive metonymy (al-kinaya al-ta'ridiyya), as an allusion to the Muslims. It is also an insinuation (talwihiyya), because of the hidden meaning in the necessary implication of the statement.

Some exegetes interpreted ﴿yarjun﴾ (hope) as meaning ﴿yakhafun﴾ (fear). This is an interpretation of the resulting meaning, not an interpretation of the word itself.

The verb ﴿kanu﴾ (they were) indicates that the absence of their hope for the reckoning is a quality firmly established in their souls, and they are characterised by it. The verb ﴿kanu﴾ is not meant to imply that they were thus and then it ceased, because this sentence is a report about them at the time the verse was revealed, while they were in this world, and it is not something said to them or about them on the Day of Resurrection.

The verb ﴿yarjun﴾ is used in the present tense to indicate the continuity of the negation of what is expressed by hope, because whenever the mention of the Day of Reckoning was repeated to them, they renewed their denial of it and repeated their doubts about its possibility, for they said ﴿We only assume an assumption, and we are not certain﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 32].

Al-hisab (reckoning) means counting (al-add), that is, counting deeds and holding [people] accountable for their recompense. That is, they do not hope for the occurrence of a reckoning over the deeds of the servants on the Day of Gathering.

﴿Kadhdhabu﴾ (they denied) is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿la yarjun﴾ (they do not hope). That is: ﴿and indeed they denied Our signs﴾, meaning the signs of the Qur'an.

The meaning is: they denied what the signs contained of affirming the Oneness [of God] and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Because their denial of this had become firmly settled in their souls and they had never wavered about it, the past tense verb was used for it, since they said ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

Kiddhab (with a kasra on the initial kaf and a shadda on the dhal) is the verbal noun of kadhdhaba. The pattern fi'al (with a kasra on the first letter and a shadda on the middle letter) is a verbal noun of fa''ala, like tafil. Its parallels are: al-qissar, the verbal noun of qassara; al-qida', the verbal noun of qadda; al-khirraq, the verbal noun of kharraqa (the doubled form); and al-fissar, the verbal noun of fassara. It is reported from al-Farra' that the origin of this verbal noun is from the Yemeni dialect, meaning that the Arabs also spoke it. They recited for a man of Banu Kilab:

*"Indeed, you have long hindered me from my companions and from needs whose fulfilment [would have been] a cure for me."*

This verbal noun was preferred here over tadhib (the regular verbal noun) for the sake of maintaining rhyme-correspondence (tamathul) in the verse endings (fawasil) of this surah, for it follows the pattern of the alif al-ta'sis in rhymes (qawafi). The verse endings are like rhymed prose (asja'), and whatever is pleasing in rhymed prose is also pleasing in rhymes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 29:

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a Book.﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD) placed between the sentences that were brought in the manner of giving a reason (ta'lil), and the sentence "﴿So taste⦆" (fadhuqu). The benefit of this parenthetical statement is to open with informing them that nothing of their deeds is hidden from Allah, so He leaves none of their misdeeds unaccounted for, whether mentioned here or not. It is as if it was said: they did not expect a reckoning and they denied Our signs, and they did other things beyond that, and all of that is enumerated with Us.

The word "kull" (everything) is in the accusative as the direct object of "aḥṣaynāhu" (We have enumerated it), by way of the construction of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with its pronoun).

Al-iḥṣā' (enumeration) means calculating things in order to fix their number; so iḥṣā' is a metaphor (kinayah) for precise control and recording.

The word "kitāban" (as a book) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) of "aḥṣaynāhu", the implied sense being: an enumeration of writing. It is a verbal noun with the meaning of writing, and it is a metaphor (kinayah) for the intensity of precise control, because written matters are preserved from forgetting and neglect. Thus, insofar as it is a metaphor for control, it came as an absolute object of "aḥṣaynā".

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 30:

﴿So taste [it]; We shall not increase you except in punishment.﴾

The fa' (fa) here indicates sequence and causation (al-tafri' wa al-tasabbub) following the clause ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever awaiting﴾ [al-Naba': 21] and what is connected to it. When the style of the report was changed from the third person (al-ghaybah) to the second person (al-khitab), after having been in the third person, and since the content of the report is not something that occurs in this world, so that it might be thought to be a threat addressed to the polytheists, it became necessary that the element being derived (al-mufarra') be an implied statement (qawl mahdhuf), indicated by the verb "taste" (dhuqu), which is only said on the Day of Recompense.

So the estimation is: "It will be said to them: Taste..." and so on. For this reason, there is no shift (iltifat) in the pronoun of address; the element derived by the fa' is the verb of the implied saying.

The imperative in dhuqu is used for rebuke and reproach (al-tawbikh wa al-taqri').

Derived from "fadhuqu" is what intensifies their distress and despair by informing them that Allah will increase them in punishment beyond what they are in.

Ziyadah (increase) means adding something to something else of the same kind or the same purpose. The Exalted said: ﴿So it added to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], and He said ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in ruin﴾ [Nuh: 28], meaning: do not increase them—in addition to the evils they are in—except in destruction.

The increase negated in His saying ﴿So We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾ may be an increase of a different kind of punishment that they will have, as in His saying: ﴿We increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

It may also be an increase of the same kind as what they are in, by its repetition in the future.

The meaning is: "So We shall increase you in punishment, an increase continuing into future times." This meaning was expressed by this precise construction: it begins with the negation of increase using a particle that makes the negation perpetual, and is followed by an exception that implies the affirmation of the opposite of the judgment of what is excepted from what is excepted from. Thus the implication of the exception became: "We shall increase you in punishment eternally." This is the emphasis of a thing by what resembles its opposite, and it is a striking style of emphasis, since it contains no repetition of a word, for the increase of punishment is an emphasis of the punishment that has already occurred.

Since the intended meaning is a threat of increased punishment in the future, the negation is expressed with the particle of future negation, "lan," which indicates the emphasis of the negated relation, namely what is conveyed by the combination of negation and exception. The restriction of perpetuity of the negation of increase, which the particle "lan" conveys on the side of what is excepted from, extends to the affirmation of increased punishment on the side of the exception, so the meaning of the exceptive clause becomes: "We shall increase you in punishment forever," which is the meaning of abiding in punishment. In this style there is a hopeful beginning with a despairing end, and that is more grievous and distressing, since it leads them to think that what they have been cast into is the limit of torment, until, when this reaches their hearing and they grieve over it, they are told that another, more severe punishment awaits them, so that it is grief upon grief. This is the pattern of this composition, and it indicates the intensity of anger.

It is related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Abu Barzah al-Aslami, and Abu Hurayrah that this verse is the most severe of what was revealed concerning the people of the Fire. This has been ascribed to the Prophet ﷺ in a hadith from Abu Barzah al-Aslami: "I asked the Prophet ﷺ about the most severe verse in the Book of Allah concerning the people of the Fire? He said: The saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment.﴾" In its chain is Jisr ibn Farqad, who is extremely weak (da'if jiddan).

In Ibn 'Atiyyah: that Abu Hurayrah narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ, but Ibn 'Atiyyah did not mention its chain, and the multiplicity of its routes gives it strength.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 31–36:

﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of triumph,﴾ ﴿gardens and grapevines,﴾ ﴿and maidens of equal age,﴾ ﴿and a cup overflowing.﴾ ﴿They will hear therein no vain talk or lying,﴾ ﴿as a reward from your Lord, a gift computed.﴾

This transition follows the Qur'an's usual pattern of following a warning to the warned with good tidings for those who are deserving of good tidings.

Thus the discourse moves from frightening the disbelievers with what they will encounter to encouraging the righteous (al-muttaqun) regarding what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter of honour and of safety from what the people of polytheism fell into.

So the sentence is connected to the sentence ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lookout,﴾ [An-Naba': 21] ﴿a place of return for the transgressors,﴾ [An-Naba': 22], and it is resumed as a fresh, initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) occasioned by the requirement of the transition.

Its opening with the particle (inna) serves to indicate concern with the report, so that no one doubts it.

By "the righteous" (al-muttaqun) is meant the believers who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), followed what he commanded them, and avoided what he forbade them, because they are the intended group when contrasted with the transgressing polytheists.

Al-mafaz: the place of winning (fawz), which is attaining success with good and gaining what is sought. It may also be a mimi verbal noun meaning fawz (triumph), and its tanwin is for magnification.

The placing of the predicate of (inna) before its subject is for emphasis on it, to draw attention to the righteous.

What is meant by al-mafaz is Paradise and its bliss. The word (mafazan) is preferred over the word "Paradise" because its derivation evokes regret in the hearts of those addressed, in His words: ﴿so you will come forth in multitudes﴾ [An-Naba': 18] and His words: ﴿So taste; We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ [An-Naba': 30].

(Hada'iq) is substituted for (mafazan) as a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull), considering that it is a part of the place of triumph, or as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) considering the meaning of triumph.

Al-hada'iq: plural of hadiqah, which is a garden of palm trees and trees with trunks enclosed by a wall, a fence, or enclosures.

Al-a'nab: plural of 'inab, a term applied to the grapevine plant and also applied to its fruit.

Al-kawa'ib: plural of ka'ib, which is the girl who has reached the age of fifteen years or near it. She is described as kā'ib because her breasts have become (taka''aba), i.e., became like a knuckle (ka'b), meaning rounded and protruding. It is said: ka'abat (from the pattern qa'ada), and it is said: ka''abat with the 'ayn doubled. Since kā'ib is a description specific to women, the feminine marker ta' was not attached to it, and it was pluralized according to the pattern fawa'il.

Al-atrab: plural of tirb (with a kasra then sukun), which is one who is equal to another in age, and it is most often applied to females. It is said: it is derived from al-turab (dust); it is said: because at birth it falls upon the dust just like the other, or because the tirb grows up with his birth-mate in the years of childhood playing in the dust.

It is also said: it is derived from al-taraib (ribs), by way of likeness in equality to the taraib, which are the ribs of the chest, for they are equal.

Al-atrab was mentioned before in His words: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 37] in Surat al-Waqi'ah. So it is possible that their description as atrab relates to equality of age among them, for increased beauty; that is, none of them surpasses another, so the soul does not incline toward one of them more than toward another, so that some of them would give less pleasure to the man.

It is also possible that this description refers to equality between them and their husbands, because that is more beloved to men in the customary practice of the people of this world, since it is more conducive to dispensing with pretense between the spouses, and that is the sweetest companionship.

Al-ka's: a vessel prepared for drinking wine; it is a feminine noun, and it may be made of glass, of silver, or of gold. It is perhaps mentioned in the lexicons that al-ka's is the glass in which there is the drink, but I have not found that it has a specific shape distinguishing it from the qadah (goblet), the kub (cup), or the kuz (jug). I have also not found in the dictionaries a definition of al-ka's as "the vessel of wine" and that the vessel is the ka's as long as the drink is in it, and this implies that it is not restricted to one kind of vessel.

They may apply the name ka's to wine itself, and by ka's is meant the genus, since the meaning is "and cups" (aka'san). The plural form was avoided because ka'san in the singular is lighter than ak'as and ku'us, and because this compound has become like a proverb, as will come.

Dihaq: a verbal noun of dahaqa (pattern ja'ala), or a verbal noun of adhqa. Because it was originally a verbal noun, it is not accompanied by a feminine marker.

Al-dahq and al-idhaq mean filling the vessel from the abundance of what is poured into it.

Describing the cup as dihaq is the use of the verbal noun for the object, like al-khalq meaning the created thing, for the cup is mudhaqah (filled), not dahiqah.

The compound (ka's dihaq) functions like a proverb. 'Ikrimah said: Ibn 'Abbas said: I heard my father in the Jahiliyyah saying: "Give us a cup overflowing (ka'san dihaqa)." That is why the singular ka's is used, and its meaning is "filled with wine," that is, without stinginess, because wine was scarce, so the tavern-keeper would not pour for the drinker except by a measure; when the cup was full, that was more pleasing to the drinker.

His words: ﴿They will hear therein no vain talk or lying﴾ may have the pronoun in (fīhā) referring to the cup, so that (fī) is for figurative inclusion, by likening the drinking companions' taking of the drink from the cup to their being within the cup by way of metonymy (makniyyah), and the particle (fī) is imaginative (takhyili). Or (fī) may be for causation, as in the hadith: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat" (dakhalat imra'ah al-nar fī hirrah), i.e., because of a cat. The meaning is: they will not hear from it or near it any vain talk or lying, so the sentence is a second description of (ka's). What is intended by it is that the wine of Paradise is free from the effects of the wine of this world, of raving, lying, and reviling, and vain talk and lying are among the defects that befall those in whose heads the wine circulates. That is, the people of Paradise are given the pleasure of intoxication known in this world before the prohibition of wine, and the wine does not affect their psychological perfections as the wine of this world does.

The Arabs used to praise one who restrains himself from vain talk and the like while drinking wine. 'Umarah ibn al-Walid said:

"We are not among those who drink, O Umm 'Amr, when they become intoxicated, the garments of the companions among them are like spoils,
but we, O Umm 'Amr, our companion is like the one who floats and does not sink."

Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari was among those who forbade wine to himself in the Jahiliyyah, and he said:
"Indeed wine exposes its drinkers, and brings upon them a great calamity."

It is also possible that the pronoun in (fīhā) refers to (mafazan) by way of interpreting it as Paradise, since it occurs in opposition to (Hell) in His words: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lookout﴾ [An-Naba': 21], or because (hada'iq) was substituted for (mafazan). This meaning arose from the style of the composition of the speech, where ﴿gardens and grapevines﴾ etc. was placed first and ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾ was placed later, so that when the pronoun (fīhā) came after that, it could refer back to the cup or to the place of triumph, as you have learned. This is from the excellence of concise expression together with abundance of meanings, of what we enumerated of the aspects of inimitability on the side of style in the tenth introduction of this commentary. Al-ka's: a vessel prepared for drinking wine; it is a feminine noun, and it may be made of glass, of silver, or of gold. It is perhaps mentioned in the lexicons that al-ka's is the glass in which there is the drink, but I have not found that it has a specific shape distinguishing it from the qadah (goblet), the kub (cup), or the kuz (jug). I have also not found in the dictionaries a definition of al-ka's as "the vessel of wine" and that the vessel is the ka's as long as the drink is in it, and this implies that it is not restricted to one kind of vessel.

They may apply the name ka's to wine itself, and by ka's is meant the genus, since the meaning is "and cups" (aka'san). The plural form was avoided because ka'san in the singular is lighter than ak'as and ku'us, and because this compound has become like a proverb, as will come.

Dihaq: a verbal noun of dahaqa (pattern ja'ala), or a verbal noun of adhqa. Because it was originally a verbal noun, it is not accompanied by a feminine marker.

Al-dahq and al-idhaq mean filling the vessel from the abundance of what is poured into it.

Describing the cup as dihaq is the use of the verbal noun for the object, like al-khalq meaning the created thing, for the cup is mudhaqah (filled), not dahiqah.

The compound (ka's dihaq) functions like a proverb. 'Ikrimah said: Ibn 'Abbas said: I heard my father in the Jahiliyyah saying: "Give us a cup overflowing (ka'san dihaqa)." That is why the singular ka's is used, and its meaning is "filled with wine," that is, without stinginess, because wine was scarce, so the tavern-keeper would not pour for the drinker except by a measure; when the cup was full, that was more pleasing to the drinker.

His words: ﴿They will hear therein no vain talk or lying﴾ may have the pronoun in (fīhā) referring to the cup, so that (fī) is for figurative inclusion, by likening the drinking companions' taking of the drink from the cup to their being within the cup by way of metonymy (makniyyah), and the particle (fī) is imaginative (takhyili). Or (fī) may be for causation, as in the hadith: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat" (dakhalat imra'ah al-nar fī hirrah), i.e., because of a cat. The meaning is: they will not hear from it or near it any vain talk or lying, so the sentence is a second description of (ka's). What is intended by it is that the wine of Paradise is free from the effects of the wine of this world, of raving, lying, and reviling, and vain talk and lying are among the defects that befall those in whose heads the wine circulates. That is, the people of Paradise are given the pleasure of intoxication known in this world before the prohibition of wine, and the wine does not affect their psychological perfections as the wine of this world does.

The Arabs used to praise one who restrains himself from vain talk and the like while drinking wine. 'Umarah ibn al-Walid said:

"We are not among those who drink, O Umm 'Amr, when they become intoxicated, the garments of the companions among them are like spoils,
but we, O Umm 'Amr, our companion is like the one who floats and does not sink."

Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari was among those who forbade wine to himself in the Jahiliyyah, and he said:
"Indeed wine exposes its drinkers, and brings upon them a great calamity."

It is also possible that the pronoun in (fīhā) refers to (mafazan) by way of interpreting it as Paradise, since it occurs in opposition to (Hell) in His words: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lookout﴾ [An-Naba': 21], or because (hada'iq) was substituted for (mafazan). This meaning arose from the style of the composition of the speech, where ﴿gardens and grapevines﴾ etc. was placed first and ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾ was placed later, so that when the pronoun (fīhā) came after that, it could refer back to the cup or to the place of triumph, as you have learned. This is from the excellence of concise expression together with abundance of meanings, of what we enumerated of the aspects of inimitability on the side of style in the tenth introduction of this commentary. That is: they will not hear in Paradise low speech or lying.

When the people of Hell were surrounded by the most severe harm with all their senses, from the burning of the Fire and being given to drink boiling water and ghassaq, so that the punishment would reach their inner selves as it reached their outer bodies, likewise He negated for the people of Paradise the least of harms, which is the harm of hearing what people dislike, for that is the least of harms.

The negation of vain talk and lying from the drinkers of the wine of Paradise is expressed by saying that they will not hear vain talk and lying therein, because if there were vain talk and lying there, they would hear it. This is of the type of the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Over a broad road whose landmark cannot be followed,"
meaning: there is no landmark in it by which one may be guided. This is a kind of subtle kinayah (metonymy). What is in the verse is better than what occurs in the verse of Imru' al-Qays and the like, because it contains an allusion that the ears of the people of Paradise are purified from fallen speech and low talk, as in His words in Surat al-Waqi'ah: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk or sinning﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 25].

Al-laghw: worthless speech, idle talk, and fallen words that are uttered without deliberation or reflection.

Al-kidhdhab: its meaning has been mentioned just above.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (kidhdhaban) here with shaddah. Al-Kisa'i read it here with the dhal lightened. (Jaza'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from (mafazan).

The origin of jaza' is the verbal noun of jaza (to recompense), and it is applied to that by which one is recompensed, by applying the verbal noun to the object. So jaza' here means that by which one is recompensed, namely the gardens, the Gardens, the maidens, and the cup.

Jaza': giving something as an exchange for a deed. It is possible that jaza' be taken in its original verbal-noun meaning and be in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) replacing an implied verb. The estimate: "We recompensed the righteous."

The idafah of (Rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee, with the Prophet (ﷺ) intended, is to indicate that the recompense of the righteous includes honouring the Prophet (ﷺ), because the bestowal of these blessings upon the righteous was for the sake of their faith in him and their acting upon what he guided them to.

And (min) is for origin, i.e., issuing from the presence of Allah, and that is a declaration of the nobility of this recompense and the greatness of its rank.

The description of the recompense as (ata'an), which is a name for what is given, i.e., bestowed as a favour without exchange, is to indicate that what they were rewarded with is greater than what they did. So what was mentioned for the righteous of triumph and what is in it as recompense was thanks to them, and gift, generosity from Allah the Exalted, and honour for this community, since its reward was made manifold.

Hisaban: a verbal noun of hasaba (with fatha on the sin) — yahsibu (with damma) — when one counts things. All derivatives of the root h-s-b branch from the meaning of counting and estimating a quantity, so (hisaban) is a description of (jaza'), that is: it is an abundant recompense estimated according to their deeds.

The tanwin on it is for abundance, and the description by the verbal noun is for emphasis, and it has the meaning of the object,

that is: computed, estimated according to their deeds. This is the counterpart of what occurred in the recompense of the transgressors in His words: ﴿a recompense in accordance﴾ [An-Naba': 26].

This reckoning is here general, and it is explained by His words: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [Al-An'am: 160], and His words: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed which grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 261].

This reckoning is not for guarding against exceeding a specified limit; for that there is another usage, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10]. Each verse has its own context in which the usage of its words operates, so there is no contradiction between the two verses.

It is also possible that (hisaban) is a verbal noun of ahsabahu, when one gives him what suffices him; so it means ihsaban, for sufficiency is called hasb (with sukun on the sin), since when one gives someone what suffices him, he says: "hasbi" (it is enough for me).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 37:

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful﴾

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a nominative ending (raf') and (al-Rahmanu) with a nominative ending. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub read both with a genitive ending (khafd). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (Rabbi) with a genitive ending and (al-Rahmanu) with a nominative ending. As for the reading in which both words are in the nominative, (Rabbu) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), which is a pronoun referring back to his saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, following the method of omitting the topic of the sentence (hadhf al-musnad ilayhi), which al-Sakkaki called "omission" (hadhf), in accordance with the usage that is established by leaving it out. That is, in the situation in which the usage of eloquent speakers runs on omitting the subject of the sentence, namely when an attribute (wasf) or the like occurs in speech for a described subject, and then something occurs that could be a predicate about it or an attribute of it, so the speaker chooses to make it a predicate rather than an attribute. He then supposes a pronoun for the described noun and brings a predicate about it, which is what is called the "detached attribute" (al-na't al-maqta').

The meaning: Indeed your Lord is their Lord, because He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, but the polytheists worshipped other than Him out of ignorance and disbelief in His blessing. And (al-Rahmanu) is a second predicate.

As for the reading in which both words are in the genitive, it proceeds on the basis that ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ is an attribute of (Rabbika) from His saying: ﴿a reward from your Lord﴾ [al-Naba' 36], and (al-Rahmanu) is a second attribute.

Page 49

Al-Rabb: the owner who disposes (al-malik al-mutasarrif) by management and by attending to kindness and mercy. What is meant by the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them is their named entities together with the existing things within them, because the name of a place may be used to mean its inhabitants, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, so it lies in ruins upon its foundations﴾ [al-Hajj: 45] in Surat al-Hajj. Wrongdoing is an attribute of the people of the town, not an attribute of the town itself, and lying in ruins upon its foundations is a condition of the town itself, not of its people. So the word "town" was meant to include both meanings.

What is meant by what is between the heavens and the earth: the creatures on the earth, the angels in the heavens, what none knows in detail except God, and what is in the atmosphere of created things, living and otherwise, such as clouds, rain, and existing things floating in the air.

"Ma" (whatever) is a relative pronoun and it is one of the forms of generality, and from this is derived the generalisation of His lordship over all created things.

The description "Lord of the heavens" is followed by the mention of one of His beautiful names, namely al-Rahman, and it was singled out for mention over the other beautiful names, because its meaning contains an indication that what He bestows of good upon the God-fearing in Paradise is the gift of the Merciful toward them.

In mentioning this sublime attribute there is an allusion against the polytheists, since they denied the name al-Rahman, which occurs in the Qur'an, as God related of them in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60].

* * *

﴿They have no power to address Him﴾

This sentence may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from (what is between them), because what is between the heavens and the earth includes created beings that have reason, or those supposed to have reason such as idols, so it may be imagined that among those creatures is one who can address God and dispute with Him.

It may also be an independent initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) to refute the claims of the polytheists, or as a precaution to repel the supposition that the sense of mercy implied by the relative clause of "Rabb" in managing the affairs of those who are nurtured would make it permissible for them to address the Lord.

Page 50

The "owning" (al-milk) in His saying: ﴿They have no power to address Him﴾ means ability and capacity, because the owner disposes of what he owns according to his own desire, not the desire of another, so he does not need another's permission. So the negation of ownership is a negation of ability.

His saying (minhu) ("from Him") is a circumstantial element (hal) of (khitaban) ("address"). Its original status was an attribute of "khitab," but when it preceded the thing it described it became a circumstantial element.

The particle (min) is of the "connective" type (ittisaliyyah), and it is a kind of the "initial" (ibtida'iyyah) in a figurative sense, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power for you against God in anything"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. So the first "min" is connective and the second is for emphasis of the text. From this is the saying: "I am not from you and you are not from me." And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does that has nothing from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28], meaning: they have no ability to address God in a way that conveys it to Him.

The subject of (they have no power) refers back to the relative pronoun "ma" in His saying: ﴿and whatever is between them﴾, because it applies to all of them.

"Khitab" (address): speech directed to someone present before the speaker, or one treated as present, containing information, a request, or an utterance of praise or blame.

The verb (yamlikun) is general because it occurs in a context of negation, as an indefinite noun in negation is general. And (khitaban) is also general. Both belong to the general that is specified by a separate specifier, such as His saying after this verse: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is correct﴾ [al-Naba': 38], and His saying: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105], and His saying: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28].

The purpose of mentioning this is to refute the excuse of the polytheists when they sensed the monstrousness of their worship of the idols, which the Qur'an denounced, so they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18], and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 38:

Page 51
﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows; none shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he shall say what is right.﴾
(Yawma) is connected to His saying: ﴿They will not have power to address Him.﴾ [al-Naba: 37], meaning: on that day no one will speak except one whom Allah has permitted.

The clause ﴿They will not speak﴾ is an emphatic restatement of the clause ﴿They will not have power to address Him﴾ [al-Naba: 37]. It is repeated with the same meaning in order to confirm the meaning, since the context is one of seriousness. The confirmation aims to reach, through it, an implication that refutes the claim of the polytheists that their idols would intercede for them with Allah. This implication is by way of fahwa (implicit inference), for when their speaking without permission is negated, their intercession is negated too, since intercession is the speech of one who has standing and acceptance with the one who hears it.

The exception is built upon this, because of the distance between the excepted element and the element excepted from, given the intervening elements attached to (they have power): a prepositional phrase, a direct object, an adverbial phrase, and a clause that is added to it.

The pronoun in (they speak) refers back to what the pronoun in (they have power) refers to.

The discussion of the specification in ﴿They will not speak﴾ is like the discussion of the specification in ﴿They will not have power to address Him﴾ [al-Naba: 37]. And His saying ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ is an exception from the pronoun in ﴿They will not speak﴾. Since it is an emphasis of the pronoun in ﴿They will not have power﴾ [al-Naba: 37], the exception from it conveys the exception from what it emphasizes.

Al-qiyam (standing) means standing upright, and it is a state of readiness for earnest action, and it is among the states of true servitude that is not due except to Allah the Exalted. In the hadith: "Whoever loves that men should stand before him, let him take his seat in the Fire" (meaning: because that is among the pride that belongs exclusively to Allah the Exalted).

Al-ruh (the Spirit): its intended meaning has been disputed, a dispute prompted by the conjunction of the angels with it. It is said: it is Jibril. Its specification by mention before the angels, who are conjoined to it, is to honour its rank by its conveying of the Sharia. It is also said: the intended meaning is the spirits of the children of Adam.

The lam is for the definition of the genus, so the singular and plural are the same with it, and the meaning is: the Day when the spirits are brought

Page 52
to be deposited in their bodies. On this basis the verb (stands) is used in both its literal and figurative senses.
And (the angels) is conjoined to (the Spirit), meaning: and the angels stand in rows.

Al-saff (row) is a name for things located in a place where some of them are alongside others, like a line. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿Then come forward in a row﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64] in Surat Ta-Ha, and in His saying: ﴿Remember the name of Allah over them as they stand in rows﴾ [al-Hajj: 36] in Surat al-Hajj. It is a naming by the verbal noun, from the use of the verbal noun in place of the active participle; originally it was for emphasis, and then it became a noun. People only line up in situations in which a great matter is at stake, so the rows of the angels are an exaltation of Allah and a submission to Him.

Al-idhn (permission) is a name for the speech that conveys the permissibility of an act for the one permitted. It is derived from: adhina lahu, when he listened to him. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it has submitted﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 2], meaning: it listened and obeyed the will of Allah. Adhina is a verb derived from the noun udhn (ear), which is the organ of hearing. The original meaning of adhina lahu is: he inclined his ear, i.e., his hearing, towards him. It is said: adhina ya'dhanu adhanan, like fariha. Then it was used for the necessary consequence of hearing, which is consent to what is heard, so adhina came to mean "consented to what is asked of him, or what it is proper to ask of him, and permitted his act." Its verbal noun is idhn with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the dhal, so the difference in the form of the two verbal nouns seems intended to distinguish between the two meanings.

The object of adhina is omitted, indicated by ﴿they will not speak﴾, meaning: one whom He has permitted to speak.

The meaning of "the Most Merciful permitted": that whoever wishes to speak is unable to do so, or awe seizes him, so he does not proceed to speak until he asks Allah for permission, and He grants it to him. He only asks for permission when Allah inspires him to ask, for inspiration is, according to the people of unveiling (kashf), a permission in the matter of the otherworldly action. When Allah casts into the soul that it should ask permission, he asks Allah, and He grants it to him, as occurred in the hadith of intercession concerning the prophets' reluctance to intercede for people until they come to Muhammad ﷺ. He said in the hadith: "So I go and come beneath the Throne and fall prostrate before my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. Then Allah opens for me praises and fine words of commendation of Him, such as He has not opened for anyone before me. Then He says: Raise your head, and intercede, and it will be granted."

This is what His saying indicated: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28], meaning: for one whom they know

Page 53
that Allah has approved accepting intercession for, and they know that by an inspiration which is of the category of revelation, since inspiration in that world is not subject to error.

The clause ﴿and he shall say what is right﴾ may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun, meaning: and the one permitted to speak has said what is right, i.e., by Allah's permission for him to speak, when He knows that he will speak what pleases Allah.

It may also be conjoined to the clause ﴿whom the Most Merciful permitted﴾, meaning: except one who says what is right, so it is known that one who does not say what is right is not permitted.

The verb in ﴿and he said what is right﴾ is used in the sense of the present, meaning: and he says what is right, and it is expressed in the past tense to convey that this is certain, i.e., in the knowledge of Allah.

The application of the attribute al-Rahman to the station of majesty (al-jalal) is an allusion to the fact that Allah's permission for one to speak is one of the effects of His mercy, because He permits in that which brings benefit to the people of the gathering, by way of intercession or seeking forgiveness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 78, verse 39:

﴿That Day is the Truth. So whoever wills may take a return (ma'ab) to his Lord.﴾

It is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), serving as a summation (fadhlaka) of what preceded of threat and promise, warning and glad tidings. It is brought in to emphasize (tanwih) the Day of Decision (yawm al-fasl), with which the discourse began from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾ [An-Naba': 17]. The purpose is to highlight the magnitude of what takes place on that Day of recompense, reward and punishment, which is the outcome of people's deeds from the day of the existence of man on earth.

The description of the Day as "the Truth" (al-haqq) may mean that it is the established, certain occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, the Recompense is certainly going to occur﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 6], and His saying a moment earlier: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾ [An-Naba': 17]. In that case al-haqq carries the sense of "established," as in His saying: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 97].

It may also mean the opposite of falsehood (al-batil), i.e., justice and the decisive judgment. Then describing the Day with it is a metaphor of the rational kind (majaz 'aqli), since the truth occurs in it and "the Day" is its container (zarf). He, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will decide between you﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 3].

It may also mean "deserving of the name": al-haqq in the sense of ḥaqīq (fitting, worthy) of the designation "day." This is because the name "day" became commonly applied to a day on which one tribe triumphed over another, such as the Day of Halimah and the Day of Bu'ath. The meaning is: that is the Day which truly deserves to be called a "day," unlike the days of people's victories over one another in this world. This is like His saying: ﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain﴾ [At-Taghabun: 9]. It is the Day of God's vengeance upon His enemies who denied His favour and associated others with Him in divinity. The description of the Truth then carries a meaning similar to that in His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recite it with its true recitation; those believe in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 121], i.e., true recitation (al-tilawa al-haqiqiyya) in the name of recitation, which is recitation with understanding of the meanings of what is recited and its purposes.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to "the Day" mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾ [An-Naba': 17]. The function of the demonstrative in such a context is to draw attention to the fact that the thing indicated is deserving of what will be described of it, because of what has preceded of the account of its circumstances, as in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 5], after His saying: ﴿A guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 2], up to His saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 4]. So, because of all that has been attributed to the Day of Decision, it is deserving of being described as "the Day, the Truth," and of what follows from that in His saying: ﴿So whoever wills may take a return to his Lord.﴾

The definiteness of "the Day" with the article (al-) serves to indicate perfection: that it is the greatest among the days which people reckon as days of victory for the victors, because it is a day on which all people are gathered and each is given what he deserves of good or evil. As for the other famous days in human history, it is as though they had not truly occurred.

The clause ﴿So whoever wills may take a return to his Lord﴾ is linked to this by the explanatory fa' (fa' al-fasiha), since it reveals a conditional clause implied by the preceding discourse. The implied sense is: "Now that you know all of that, whoever wishes to take a place of return with his Lord, let him take it." That is, what good and evil that Day holds has now become clear to you, so let the one who has the will choose what befits him for his destination on that Day. The implied complement is: a return therein, i.e., in the Day.

This connective is among the most eloquent forms of exhortation, through encouragement and warning, when an opportunity arises for the preacher, since souls are then prepared to accept admonition.

Ittikhadh (taking) is an intensified form of akhadh (taking), meaning one takes hold with a firmness that resembles the reflexive (mutawa'a) in its establishment; the ta' in it is therefore not the true reflexive but a metaphorical usage that has become like the original form. Ittikhadh means acquiring and making: that one should secure a place by believing and doing righteous deeds, so as to attain a station with God, since the return to Him can only be good.

So His saying "to His Lord" indicates that it is a return of good, because God is pleased only with good.

Ma'ab may be a noun of place from aba (to return), when one returns, and so it is applied to a dwelling, since a person returns (ya'ub) to his dwelling. It may also be a mimi verbal noun, namely al-awb, meaning return, as in His saying: ﴿To Him I call, and to Him is my return﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 36], i.e., my return. So the meaning is: let him make for himself a return suitable for meeting his Lord, that is, a good return.

**Ibn ʿAshur's commentary on Surah 78, verse 40:**

﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment.﴾

This is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical sentence) placed between ﴿a place of return﴾ [al-Naba: 39] and ﴿the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forward﴾. Wherever that temporal phrase (ẓarf) is placed, as will be explained below, the clause remains parenthetical.

The purpose of this sentence is to establish the proof against the addressees (iʿdhār) through the calamities of this surah, so that no doubt or obscurity remains for them regarding the knowledge of the causes of salvation and their opposites.

The statement, ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, is used to cut off their excuse, not to convey new information, because the fact that what preceded was a warning is already known to the addressees. The statement opens with the emphatic particle (inna) to intensify the establishment of proof, treating them as one who doubts it.

The predicate is a verb attached to the separate pronoun (ʾanā/naḥnu, "We"), to convey a meaning that strengthens the judgment. It also presents the speaker as one who disclaims responsibility for any harm that may befall the addressees if they do not take precaution against what he has warned them of. This resembles the saying of the warner (nadhīr) among the Arabs after warning of an enemy: "I am the naked warner" (anā al-nadhīr al-ʿuryān).

Warning (inʿdhār, al-indhār) is the report of the occurrence of what will cause harm in the near future.

It is expressed in the past tense because the greatest part of the warning has already taken place through what preceded it, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying in wait﴾ [al-Naba: 21], ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾ [al-Naba: 22], up to His saying: ﴿So We will increase you only in punishment﴾ [al-Naba: 30].

The nearness of the punishment is used metaphorically to mean its certainty; otherwise, by customary standards, it is distant. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, they see it as distant, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 6], meaning that because of its certainty, it is as though it were near. The punishment may refer to the punishment of the Hereafter, which was the subject of the warning mentioned earlier, and it may also refer to the punishment of this world, such as killing and capture in the battles of the Muslims against the polytheists. It is narrated from Muqatil that it refers to the killing of the Quraysh at Badr. It also includes the punishment of the Day of the Conquest (of Mecca) and the Day of Hunayn, as the word "punishment" was used for that in His saying: ﴿God will punish them at your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, for those who have wronged, there is a punishment besides that﴾ [al-Tur: 47].

﴿The Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forward, and the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I had been dust!"﴾

It is permissible for this phrase to be connected to the verb in ﴿has taken to his Lord a place of return﴾ [al-Naba: 39], in which case ﴿the Day when he looks﴾ is a superfluous temporal phrase (ẓarf laghw) connected to (ʾandhartunākum, "We warned you").

It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks﴾ [al-Naba: 38], because the standing of the angels in ranks is the presence for the reckoning of people and the execution of the decisive judgment upon them. That is the time when a man looks at what his hands have sent forward, that is, what he did in the past. So it is a substitute for the temporal phrase, following it in its grammatical position.

In both cases, the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause placed between the temporal phrase and what it depends on, or between it and what it substitutes.

*al-Marʾ* (man) is a noun for a male, since its feminine form is *imraʾa* (woman).

Restricting the statement to *al-marʾ* follows the general usage of the Arabs in their speech, so the statement comes in the form of what is usual in address, because women were not involved in matters outside the house.

The intended meaning is: a person, male or female, looks at what his hands have sent forward. This is known from the inductive study of the Sharia, which indicates the general applicability of obligations to men and women, except what is specifically restricted to one of the two groups, because the man is the one who comes to mind for the addressees when they are addressed.

The definiteness of *al-marʾ* is for generalization (istighrāq, comprehensiveness), like His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAsr: 2], ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-ʿAsr: 3].

The verb *yanẓuru* (looks) may be from looking with the eye, that is, sight. The meaning is: the Day when a man sees what his hands have sent forward. The meaning of a man looking at what his hands have sent forward is that the recompense of his deed comes to him. It is expressed as "looking" because the recompense is necessarily visible to its owner, whether good or bad. So the use of "looking" here means finding or experiencing, in the figurative sense of a metonymy (majāz mursal) based on the relationship of generality and specificity. A parallel is His saying: ﴿so that they may be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6]. The literal sense appears in His saying: ﴿the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 30], and the rest of the verse.

The *mā* is a relative pronoun, and its relative clause is ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾.

It may also be from looking in the sense of thinking (naẓar al-fikr). Its origin is a figurative usage that became so common that it was attached to the literal meanings, as one says: "He is of the better of the two views" (huwa bi-khayr al-naẓarayn). From this comes *tanaẓẓur*, meaning anticipating something. The meaning is: the Day when a man anticipates and reflects on what his hands have sent forward. In this case, *mā* is interrogative, and the verb *yanẓuru* is suspended from acting because of the interrogative. The meaning is: a man looks for the answer to one who asks: "What have your hands sent forward?" It may also be from waiting (intiẓār), as in His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 53].

The definiteness of *al-marʾ* is the definiteness of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), which conveys comprehensiveness.

Taqdīm (sending forward) is the precedence of something and beginning with it.

﴿What his hands have sent forward﴾ means the deeds he sent ahead in this world, whether good or bad. It is not restricted to his evil deeds, since God, exalted is He, said: ﴿the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 30], and the rest of the verse.

His saying, ﴿what his hands have sent forward﴾, is either a metonymy (majāz mursal) in which the two hands stand for all instruments of deeds, or it is an illustrative expression (tamthīl), comparing the state of the doer with his various deeds to the state of a craftsman making products with his own hands, as they said in the proverb: "Your hands have tied it" (yadāka awkatā). This would also apply if it were said by his tongue or by his feet walking.

It is not appropriate to consider the mention of the two hands as taghlīb (using the dual to refer to one of its parts or to the group), because the particular feature of taghlīb is not the particular feature of the illustrative expression.

﴿What his hands have sent forward﴾ includes good and evil.

From the generality of *al-marʾ*, the disbeliever who says, ﴿Oh, I wish I had been dust!﴾ is singled out for mention, because the surah was established upon warning those who deny resurrection. That is the reason for singling him out. The meaning is: on the Day when the disbeliever wishes that he had not been created among living beings, let alone among those of intellect who are obligated by the laws. That is, he wishes to be one who does not perceive and is not sensitive, by being the least of things that have no perception, which is dust. This is an expression of anguish and regret over what his hands sent forward of disbelief.

They used to say: ﴿When we have become bones and dust, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ So God made their punishment consist of regret and wishing they were of the kind of dust.

Mentioning the description of the disbeliever implies that the believer is not like this, because even if the believer committed some evil deeds and anticipated punishment for his evil deeds, he hopes that his end will be bliss. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 30], and He said: ﴿so that they may be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6], ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7], ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 8]. Thus the believers see the reward of faith, which is the greatest reward, and the reward of their good deeds, which varies among them. They hope to arrive at that reward, and what they see of their evil deeds does not overwhelm the reward of their good deeds. So all of them hope to arrive at bliss. God has set forth for them, or for those close to them, an example in His saying: ﴿And on the heights are men who recognize each by his mark, and they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, but they aspire﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 46], according to what is said in its interpretation, with various views.

This verse comprehensively includes what came in the surah about the states of the two groups. At its end is the response of the closing part to the opening part, through mention of the states of the disbelievers who were described as "the transgressors." For this reason, ending the surah with it is an instance of excellent conclusion (barāʿat al-maqṭaʿ, skill in ending).

**In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful**

**Surah al-Naziʿat**

It is named in the copies of the Qur'an and in most tafsir works "Surat al-Naziʿat," with the word *sūrah* added to *al-Naziʿat* without a conjunction. The term *al-Naziʿat* became its proper name because it is not mentioned in any other surah. In the book of tafsir of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhari, and in many books of the exegetes, it is titled "Surat wa-al-Naziʿat," with the conjunction "wa" retained, reproducing the first words of the surah.

Saʿd Allah, famous as Saʿdi, and al-Khafaji said that it is called "Surat al-Sahirah," because the word *al-sahirah* occurs within it and does not occur in any other surah.

They also said that it is called "Surat al-Tammah." That is, because the word *al-tammah* occurs in it and does not occur in any other surah. They did not mention this in al-Itqan among the surahs that have more than one name.

I saw in a copy of the Qur'an written in a Tunisian script a title for it: "Surat Fa-al-Mudabbirat," which is strange, since the word *al-mudabbirat* occurs in it and does not occur in any other surah.

It is a Meccan surah, by consensus.

It is counted as the eighty-first in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Naba and before Surat al-Infitar.

Its number of verses is forty-five according to the majority, while the people of Kufa counted it as forty-six verses.

* * *

It includes the establishment of resurrection and recompense, and the refutation of the polytheists' denial of its occurrence.

It also includes the magnification of its Day and what people undergo of terror at that time.

It includes the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that restoring life is impossible after bodies have ceased to exist.

It alludes to the idea that their denial of it arises from their transgression. Thus transgression was an obstacle preventing them from listening to the warning of recompense, so they became secure in themselves, not anticipating a life after this worldly life. This is illustrated by making their transgression like the transgression of Pharaoh and his turning away from the call of Moses, peace be upon him. There is a lesson for them in that, and consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The discourse turns to argue for the possibility of resurrection, on the grounds that creating the worlds and arranging their order is greater than re-creating.

Within this is incorporated a reminder of the signs in the creation of the heavens and earth, which point to the great power of God, exalted is He.

Also incorporated is a reminder of His favor in creating this world with its benefits that they gather, and that when the otherworld comes and this world passes away, recompense for deeds will come, through punishment and reward.

The discourse uncovers the basis of their doubt about resurrection, which is their slowness in awaiting it, and their making this a sign of its non-existence. For this reason they ask the Messenger (ﷺ) about fixing the time of the Hour, asking in a manner of obstinacy. It is the Messenger's role to remind them of it, not to specify its appointed time. It is about to come, and they will know it directly. As if, despite the long duration, they had remained only part of a day.
